sections.name: Ch 1 — Introduction to Air Power  —  2 of 60 exam questions
cards: Dirigible
lighter than air craft that can be propelled and steered
What makes air and space power unique?
SPEED and ELEVATION — the ability to move faster than surface forces and to see and strike from above. Air and space power is the ability to take advantage of air and space to do many things.
Kite — significance
The first device to enable flight, invented by the CHINESE. May have been used in man-carrying form to spy on enemies.
Aerial reporting
(Balloon Signal Service of Union Army) Lincoln got Gen Scott to let Lowe organize it
The three basic problems of flight
(1) Developing the necessary LIFT. (2) SUSTAINING that lift. (3) CONTROLLING the aircraft once it is flying. The Wright brothers solved all three on 17 December 1903.
Leonardo da Vinci
first designs of parachute and helicopter
Francesco de Lana — what and when?
A Jesuit priest who described an AERIAL SHIP in 1670 — a boat lifted by evacuated copper spheres. Never built; the spheres would have collapsed.
Laurenco deGusmao — what and when?
A Jesuit priest who invented the HOT AIR BALLOON in 1709 — decades before the Montgolfiers flew one with passengers in 1783.
Joseph Priestley — contribution
Discovered OXYGEN. (Henry Cavendish discovered hydrogen, which he called 'flammable air', in 1766.)
Jean Pierre Blanchard, Dr. John Jeffries
flew balloon across English Channel
First successful rigid dirigible — who, what, when?
Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, the LZ-1, in 1900. Giffard built the first dirigible generally credited (1852); Santos-Dumont built 14 gasoline-powered NON-rigid airships 1898-1907.
Henri Giffard and the Renard/Krebs airship — who did what?
HENRI GIFFARD built the first dirigible generally credited, 1852 (steam powered). CHARLES RENARD and A. C. KREBS built La France, 1884 — ELECTRIC motors, and the first to return to its takeoff point.
Alberto Santos-Dumont and Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin
used internal combustion to power their craft
Alphonse Penaud — what did he build?

The PLANAPHORE, 1871 — a 20-inch model airplane powered by a TWISTED RUBBER BAND. It flew 131 FEET in 11 SECONDS. Its automatic LONGITUDINAL (front-to-back) stability was Penaud's greatest contribution to aviation.
Clement Ader
first manned craft to take off from level ground under own power
Octave Chanute
designed gliders, study and distribution of aviation history
Langley — what did he build, and what happened?

Samuel Pierpont Langley added power to a glider, producing the steam-powered AERODROME. Launched by catapult from a barge on the POTOMAC RIVER — it FAILED and fell into the river. Government support was withdrawn days before the Wrights flew.
Alberto Santos-Dumont
first powered airplane in Europe
W. H. Phillips, 1842
Built the first successful STEAM-POWERED MODEL helicopter — not a manned aircraft. The first helicopter to lift a MAN was Louis Breguet's, 1907.
Helicopters (early)
Roger Bacon, da Vinci, George Cayley
Legend: who built two sets of wings to escape imprisonment?
Daedalus (and his son Icarus). Wan Hoo is the separate legend — the wicker chair fitted with rockets.
Who invented gunpowder?
The Chinese. It enabled rockets around 1100; first used as a weapon of war in 1232.
Who may have used man-carrying kites to spy on enemies?
The Chinese.
Who developed the first known principles of flight?
Leonardo da Vinci. His manuscripts were not found and published until roughly 300 years after his death.
Torricelli, von Guericke and Pascal — what did they establish?
That atmospheric pressure DECREASES the higher you climb. Torricelli invented the barometer.
Montgolfier balloon — date, crew, duration, distance
21 November 1783. Pilatre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes. About 25 minutes, 5 miles.
First balloon flight in the United States — when and where?
1793, at Philadelphia, watched by President Washington.
Who made the first parachute jump from a balloon, and when?
Andre-Jacques Garnerin, 1797.
First US military use of balloons
The Civil War — Thaddeus S. C. Lowe's Balloon Signal Service of the Union Army.
George Cayley — what device did he use to test wing shapes?
A whirling-arm device. (Francis Wenham built the first WIND TUNNEL — do not confuse them.)
Cayley's founding statement of aeronautics
That the whole problem is to make a surface support a given weight by the application of power to the resistance of air.
Penaud's greatest contribution to aviation
Automatic LONGITUDINAL (front-to-back) STABILITY, demonstrated by his planaphore. He also used twisted rubber bands to power workable helicopter models.
John Montgomery — glider details
440-pound seagull-wing glider, carried him 600 feet. A later glider stayed aloft 20 minutes in 1905. Killed in 1911. He is NOT the 'Father of Modern Aviation' — that is Lilienthal.
Otto Lilienthal — how many glides?
Over 2,000 between 1891 and 1896, many over 700 feet. Called the Father of Modern Aviation.
Henson and Stringfellow — what and when?
1843 patent for a man-carrying powered aircraft called the ARIEL. Never built. Stringfellow flew a steam-driven model in 1848.
Langley's Aerodrome — how was it launched, and what happened?
Catapult from a barge on the Potomac. It FAILED — fell in the river twice. It was not the first airplane to fly successfully after catapult launch.
Wright brothers, 17 December 1903 — the two flights to know
First: 12 seconds, 120 feet. Later that same day: 59 seconds, 852 feet.
How many glider flights had the Wrights made by October 1902?
Over 1,000. They had solved the three basic problems and needed only a suitable power plant.
Discriminate: hydrogen vs helium as lifting gas
Hydrogen lifts well but is dangerously FLAMMABLE (Hindenburg). Helium is SAFER. Hydrogen was Cavendish's 'flammable air', 1766.
Discriminate: de Lana vs deGusmao
Both Jesuit priests. De Lana — aerial ship, 1670. DeGusmao — hot air balloon, 1709.
Discriminate: Giffard vs Zeppelin
Giffard — first successful DIRIGIBLE (1852). Zeppelin — first successful RIGID dirigible, the LZ-1 (1900). Santos-Dumont built 14 gasoline-powered non-rigid airships 1898-1907.
The legends of flight — the four to know

EMPEROR SHUN: escaped prison nearly 4,000 years ago by 'donning the work clothes of a bird.' KEI KUNG: Chinese god of thunder and lightning, flew using the wings of a BAT. KI-KUNG-SHI: 1,800 years before Christ, built a FLYING CHARIOT with no visible means of support. WAN HOO: the wicker chair fitted with rockets.

sections.name: Ch 2 — The Adolescence of Air Power: 1904-1919  —  3 of 60 exam questions
cards: Glenn Curtiss — career and contributions

Motorcycle racer turned aviator; set a motorcycle record of 136.3 mph, making him the fastest man on earth. Founded the AERIAL EXPERIMENT ASSOCIATION with Alexander Graham Bell — first American aircraft with AILERONS and the first US SEAPLANE.
Louis Bleriot
1st powered monoplane, 1st flight English Channel, 1909; also 1st international air meet, Rheims 8/22-28
Wright's contract
pilot, passenger, 125mi fuel, 36mph, perfect control, land/takeoff war zone, disassemble-able, train 2 pilots. (They also signed a French contract) 8/2/1909, first Army airplane
Multiengine
increase power, improve reliability and safety (Short bros, patent for first multiengine, 1911; Igor Sikorsky 4 engine; first practical helicopter)
St. Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line

1 JANUARY 1914 — the world's first regularly scheduled airline service using HEAVIER-THAN-AIR craft. Flown by TONY JANNUS in a twin-engine BENOIST XIV flying boat carrying TWO passengers. The 22-MILE flight across Tampa Bay cost $5 and took about 20 MINUTES.
Fighters
would shoot guns at enemy; Roland Garros mounted automatic rifle; Fokker designed interrupting gear
Ace
US, French, British: 5; Germany: 10; Rickenbacker, Fonck, Mannock, Manfred
Who built a Wright-style glider in 1904 using ailerons instead of wing warping?
Robert Esnault-Pelterie. He also produced the first fully enclosed fuselage.
Who flew the first powered aircraft in Europe?
Alberto Santos-Dumont.
Where was the first international air meet held?
Rheims, France (1909).
Lieutenant Thomas Selfridge — significance
First person killed in a powered airplane, 1908, on Orville Wright's 13th test flight.
What did the Army pay for its first airplane, 1909?
$25,000 plus a $5,000 bonus for exceeding the speed requirement.
Army specification for the Wright aircraft
Carry a pilot and passenger, fuel for 125 miles, at 36 mph. Also: perfect control, takeoff/land in a war zone, disassemblable, train two pilots.
How many times did the government turn the Wrights down before Roosevelt intervened?
Three.
Glenn Curtiss before aviation — and his record
Motorcycle racer; set a record of 136.3 mph, making him the fastest man on earth.
Who co-founded the Aerial Experiment Association with Curtiss?
Alexander Graham Bell. The AEA produced the first American aircraft with ailerons and the first US seaplane.
Curtiss aircraft and trophies — match them
June Bug → Scientific American Trophy, 1908. Golden Flyer → Gordon Bennett Trophy, 1909.
Hearst prize and Calbraith Rodgers
Hearst offered $50,000 for a transcontinental flight in 30 days. Rodgers took 49 days in the Vin Fiz — he crossed, but with MANY stops, and MISSED the prize. Not a nonstop flight.
Harriet Quimby — two firsts
First licensed American woman pilot; first woman to fly solo across the English Channel. (Not Mathilde Moisant.)
Short brothers' Triple Twin — why the name?
Two engines, three propellers. First patented multiengine design, 1911.
Igor Sikorsky's 1913 four-engine aircraft
The LeGrand.
Who built the lightweight rotary engine used by many WWI aircraft?
The Seguin brothers — the Gnome. Early aircraft engines were too HEAVY; this addressed it.
First helicopter to lift a man — who and when?
Louis Breguet, 1907 (with Paul Cornu). Emile and Henry Berliner were the first AMERICANS to build and fly one, 1909.
Why are helicopters called rotary-wing aircraft?
Because the wings (blades) rotate.
US Army air strength at the end of 1913
19 aircraft, 29 pilots. By 1914 Germany had about 200; Britain and France about 450 each.
How many American-DESIGNED combat aircraft saw action in WWI?
None. Congress promised 263 squadrons and 22,625 aircraft by June 1918; 45 squadrons were fielded, all flying British and French types.
WWI aircraft performance — start vs end of the war
Start: 70-80 mph, ceiling about 10,000 ft. End: 140-150 mph, ceiling about 24,000 ft.
First role of the airplane in WWI
Observation. Bombing came next, with crews carrying bombs in their laps.
First German bombing raids of WWI — what aircraft?
DIRIGIBLES, not the Gotha. Germany started with 20 large dirigibles and built 88 more; flown at night because they were flammable.
Ace — victory thresholds
Five for the American, French and British services. TEN for the German.
Match the aces to their countries

Rene Fonck — French ace of aces. Edward Mannock — British ace of aces. Eddie Rickenbacker — American ace of aces, 26 kills, former race car driver, only living American to receive the Medal of Honor in WWI.
Anthony Fokker — nationality and contribution
DUTCH airplane designer. Designed the synchronizing/interrupter gear. Roland Garros used deflector plates and a fuselage-mounted rifle first.
Who commanded the first mass-air bombing attack, and when?
Billy Mitchell, September 1918 — nearly 1,500 allied airplanes.
The Junkers D1, May 1918
World's first all-metal, low-wing monoplane fighter. Came too late to affect the war.
The single most important lesson of WWI
If you control the air you cannot be beaten; if you lose the air you cannot win. The US was the only nation involved that had not learned it.
Mitchell's argument for an independent air service
Separate from the Army so it could 'command the sky', then be used offensively against enemy troops.
What aircraft flew the world's first scheduled airline service?
A twin-engine BENOIST XIV flying boat, flown by Tony Jannus, carrying two passengers.

sections.name: Ch 3 — The Golden Age: 1919-1939  —  4 of 60 exam questions
cards: Barnstormers
flying exhibitor, war-surplus crafts, around country to offer rides, shows, etc.
Smith and Richter — the first aerial refueling

August 1923. Lieutenants LOWELL SMITH and J. P. RICHTER stayed airborne 37 HOURS 15 MINUTES, refueling through a 50-FOOT HOSE from another airplane. The operation was done 16 TIMES, about 50 gallons each.
Hindenburg
LZ-129. Destroyed 6 May 1937 at Lakehurst, New Jersey — hydrogen fire. First fatalities in scheduled airship service. (1937, not 1936.)
First paratroop demonstration — the details
September 1929 at BROOKS FIELD, TEXAS. Sergeant Erwin H. Nichols and a squad of 17 MEN jumped from NINE DH-4s and landed safely 3,000 FEET below.
McNary-Watres Act

contractors paid according to available cargo weight, postmaster could extend or combine mail. Airlines were: United (Boeing), and Transcontinental and Western (Douglas), American (Douglas); Douglas Commercial 3 became standard for all commercial airliners (w/o fatal accidents)
First crossing of the Atlantic by air, 1919
The US NAVY, using Curtiss flying boats (NC-4 completed it), May 1919. Alcock and Brown made the first NONSTOP crossing about two weeks later, June 1919.
How many airplanes did the US build during its 21 months in WWI?
About 15,000.
What happened to American airplane production at the end of WWI?
It dropped by about 85 percent. Within three days $100 million in contracts were cancelled; within three months 175,000 workers were laid off.
Which two groups kept American aviation alive after WWI?
The barnstormers and the Army aviators. The barnstormers' main contribution was PUBLICIZING aviation.
Reaction to Mitchell sinking the Ostfriesland
The Army and Congress were largely UNIMPRESSED. Mitchell's continued attacks led to his being relieved of command and reduced in rank to colonel.
Kelly and Macready — what was their flight?
The first successful NONSTOP transcontinental flight, 2 May 1923, in the T-2.
First aerial refueling
Smith and Richter, 1923 — kept aloft over 37 hours.
Round-the-world flight — year and aircraft names
Completed 1924, planned by Billy Mitchell. Aircraft: Boston, Chicago, Seattle, New Orleans.
When did the Army first test paratroops?
September 1929, in Texas — 17 men, in action within 4 minutes.
Pulitzer Trophy Race — origin and purpose
Began in America when Ralph Pulitzer offered a trophy to promote HIGH-SPEED flight, New York 1920. The National Air Races grew out of it; 1925 was the last Pulitzer.
Discriminate the three air races
PULITZER — high-speed, led to the National Air Races. THOMPSON (1930) — closed-course PYLON race, land-based. BENDIX (1931) — TRANSCONTINENTAL speed race. Schneider — seaplane.
Woman's Air Derby — what did it lead to?
The NINETY-NINES (not the 'Powder Puffs'), with Amelia Earhart as first president.
Who formed NACA, and when?
Woodrow Wilson, 1915. NACA scientists developed more efficient wing shapes.
Who founded the School of Aeronautics at New York University, and when?
Daniel Guggenheim, 1926.
Who developed the first practical helicopter?

IGOR SIKORSKY — the VS-300. Tethered vertical takeoffs and landings September 1939; first free flight 13 May 1940. It could carry a useful load, do productive work, and be controlled in flight. (Dr. Heinrich Focke's FA-61, 1937, was the first helicopter with complete CONTROLLABILITY — a different claim.)
THE FOUR AIR MAIL / AIR COMMERCE ACTS — discriminate

1925 AIR MAIL ACT (Kelly Act): enabled contracting; contractor paid 80% of air mail revenue; paid by WEIGHT of mail. 1926 AIR COMMERCE ACT: first attempt to STANDARDIZE AND REGULATE commercial aviation; first safety regs; Aeronautics Branch licensing. 1934 AIR MAIL ACT: authorized a thorough STUDY of commercial aviation; carriers answerable to three agencies. 1938 CIVIL AERONAUTICS ACT: UNIFIED the economic and safety regulations of the entire field; created the Civil Aeronautics Authority.
Which act first attempted to standardize and regulate commercial aviation?
The AIR COMMERCE ACT OF 1926.
Which act authorized a thorough study of commercial aviation?
The AIR MAIL ACT OF 1934.
Which act unified the economic and safety regulations of the entire field of aviation?
The AIR MAIL / CIVIL AERONAUTICS ACT OF 1938.
Which act paid the contractor 80 percent of the air mail revenue?
The AIR MAIL ACT OF 1925 (Kelly Act).
McNary-Watres Act — how did it change payment?
Carriers were paid according to AVAILABLE CARGO SPACE, which gave an incentive to fly LARGER aircraft. (The Kelly Act had paid by weight of mail actually carried.)
When did the Army begin flying air mail, and what route?
15 May 1918. First route: Washington, DC to New York. Chicago added 1919, San Francisco 1920; regular service from 1924.
How did the railroads react to air mail?
They OPPOSED it.
Lindbergh — route, aircraft, duration

Took off from ROOSEVELT FIELD, New York on 20 May 1927 in the SPIRIT OF ST. LOUIS. Flying alone through bad weather with no radio and only a simple compass, he landed at LE BOURGET Airport, Paris THIRTY-THREE AND ONE-HALF hours later. His lasting effect: he inspired thousands to enter pilot training.
Amelia Earhart — the three firsts to keep straight

First woman to cross the Atlantic as a PASSENGER (1928). First woman to fly the Atlantic SOLO (1932, landed in Ireland, 20h40m). First president of the Ninety-Nines. She did NOT complete a round-the-world flight — she disappeared attempting it, 1937.
Travel Air Manufacturing Company — year, place, founders
1925, Wichita, Kansas. Lloyd Stearman, Walter Beech and Clyde V. Cessna. All three later formed their own companies; Piper bought out Taylor Aircraft.
Doolittle, 24 September 1929
First fully blind takeoff, flight and landing on instruments alone.
DC-3 — capacity, load, range
24 passengers, or 5,000 lbs of cargo, 1,200 miles. Standard commercial airliner by the late 1930s. Boeing flew the 247; TWA the DC-2.
Pan American — formation and first route
Formed 1927; first air mail route Key West, Florida to Havana, Cuba.
Pan American's flying boats — the three to know

SIKORSKY S-40: four-engine flying boat, 125 mph, 40 passengers. SIKORSKY S-42: larger, 1,200-mile range — became known as the PAN AMERICAN CLIPPER and made the first airline crossing of BOTH the Pacific and the Atlantic. MARTIN 130: dubbed the CHINA CLIPPER; first transpacific flight 22 November 1935.
The three post-Versailles Zeppelins
LZ-127 Graf Zeppelin, LZ-129 Hindenburg, LZ-130 Graf Zeppelin II. The Treaty of VERSAILLES allowed Germany to build them again. Their decline is traced to MANY DISASTERS.
Boeing 299 — Army designation
The B-17. The Army's first long-range bomber; over 50 ordered.
Presidential message to Congress, 12 January 1939
Described America's military forces as INADEQUATE to meet threats in Europe. It triggered the prewar buildup.
Hap Arnold's answer to the prewar pilot shortage
Civilian-operated, Army-supervised flying schools. The Civilian Pilot Training Program was another source; one of its schools produced the Tuskegee Airmen.
First aerial crossing of the Atlantic — who and how?
The US NAVY, May 1919, using Curtiss flying boats — the NC-4 completed it. Three set out.
What is a barnstormer?
An ex-military pilot flying war-surplus aircraft around the country offering rides and exhibitions at county fairs, carnivals, anywhere crowds gathered.
Which two groups kept aviation alive in America after WWI?
The BARNSTORMERS and the ARMY AVIATORS.
Russell Maughan — the dawn-to-dusk flight
23 June 1924. Army Lt. Russell Maughan flew a CURTISS PW-8 coast to coast: 2,670 miles in 21 HOURS 48 MINUTES, averaging 122 mph. He landed five times to refuel, leaving New York at dawn.
Smith and Richter, 1923 — what did they achieve?
The Army's first in-flight refueling of an airplane — airborne 37 hours 15 minutes, refueled 16 times through a 50-foot hose.
Thompson Trophy — year and type
Established 1930. A closed-course PYLON race for land-based aircraft.
Bendix Trophy — year and type
Added 1931. A TRANSCONTINENTAL speed race, beginning on the west coast.
Schneider Trophy — what kind of race?
A SEAPLANE race.
What did the Civil Aeronautics Act of 1938 create?
The CIVIL AERONAUTICS AUTHORITY (CAA).
Under the Air Mail Act of 1934, how many agencies did carriers answer to?
THREE: the Post Office Department, the Aeronautics Branch of Commerce, and the Interstate Commerce Commission's Bureau of Air Mail.
Which aircraft was the first 'modern' airliner, and who flew what?
Boeing flew the 247; TWA flew the DC-2; the DC-3 became the standard by the late 1930s.
Which aircraft was the Pan American Clipper, and what was its first?
The SIKORSKY S-42 — first airline crossing of BOTH the Pacific and the Atlantic Oceans.
Who was the first woman to fly the Atlantic as a passenger?
Amelia Earhart, 1928. Her SOLO crossing came in 1932.
Civilian Pilot Training Program — what did it become, and what did it produce?
Became the CAA War Training Service after Pearl Harbor. One of its schools — Tuskegee Institute — produced the Tuskegee Airmen.
What ended Billy Mitchell's military career?
His verbal attacks on America's defense systems. He was relieved of command and reduced in rank to COLONEL.
Autogiro — who built the first?
Juan de la Cierva.
What technical improvements marked aviation in the 1920s and 30s?
Biplanes gave way to MONOPLANES; more effective wing shapes and cowlings; PRESSURIZED cabins; AIR-COOLED engines.
How many airplanes did the US build in WWI, and what happened after?
About 15,000 in 21 months. Production then dropped about 85 percent; military aviation cut back 95 percent.
What did NACA stand for and do?
National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, formed 1915 by Woodrow Wilson. Government-funded research in aeronautics; its scientists developed more efficient wing shapes.
First nonstop transcontinental flight (New York to San Diego)
Kelly and Macready, 2 May 1923, in the T-2. (1923, not 1922.)
National Advisory Committee on Aeronautics (NACA)
1915, gov funded research in aeronautics
Igor Sikorsky's flying boats — S-40 vs S-42
S-40: four-engine flying boat, 125 mph, 40 passengers. S-42: larger, 1,200-mile range, became the PAN AMERICAN CLIPPER.
Which aircraft was the China Clipper, and what did it do?
The MARTIN 130. Pan American took delivery in 1934 and dubbed it the China Clipper; on 22 November 1935 it made the first TRANSPACIFIC flight, from California via Hawaii.
Who were the first women pilots to refuel in the air?
Elinor Smith and Bobbi Trout, 1929, attempting an endurance record.
Sikorsky VS-300 — size and speed
About 1,150 pounds and 50 mph. It led to the R-4, the FIRST MILITARY HELICOPTER in the world, used in World War II.
First transatlantic crossing — the NC-4 figures

The US Navy's NC-4, May 1919. Total airline distance from Rockaway 3,936 MILES; total flying time 52 HOURS 31 MINUTES. Just two weeks later Alcock and Brown made the first NONSTOP crossing, for a $50,000 London Daily Mail prize offered in 1913.
1924 round-the-world flight — distance and flying time
26,345 MILES flown, with actual flying time of 363 HOURS 7 MINUTES.
What did the Army demonstrate about moving aircraft across the US?
That any Army aircraft located anywhere in the United States could be flown to any other location in the country in LESS THAN ONE DAY.

sections.name: Ch 4 — Air Power Goes to War  —  3 of 60 exam questions
cards: Blitzkrieg
lightning war, combined arms (long range), army/air force (incl. ME-109 fighter; American B-17 better though)
Kamikazes
suicide bombing; crashed bomb-loaded plane into ships
Pre WWII

German Luftwaffe: by 1932 3Bomber, 4Fighter, 8Observe; Italy (Germany) battle tested in Spanish Civil War, also Ethiopia; Japan, Army and Navy Air Force; we cut back; England had RAF, offensive bombers, good capabilities; France, ground defense, Maginot Line, small AF in 1936; 1940,41 we built up, but still short
Allies of World War II — who were they?
The United States, Britain, Russia (USSR) and France. HUNGARY was NOT an Ally — it was aligned with the Axis, and CAP uses it as the trap answer. The Axis was Germany, Italy and Japan.
Pearl Harbor; to cripple our fleet, air superiority, then Navy; 8-8:30 pounded; Afterwards, contact schools trained more pilots; CAA Civilian Pilot Training became CAA War Training Service
Centralized control allowed
Air superiority, interdiction (crippling), close ground support
General Kenney — Pacific tactics

Took over air operations in the Pacific. Used LOW-ALTITUDE bombing, PARAFRAG bombs (parachute-retarded fragmentation), and the "Kenney cocktail" (white phosphorus). Aim: clear the air so advancing Allies could take the islands.
Air Supremacy theory — Douhet
Massive first strike, then population
Air Supremacy theory — Trenchard
father of RAF, long range bombing, 2/3 B, 1/3 F, paralyze vital centers
Air Supremacy theory — Mitchell
destroy will to resist, 60% fighter
Air Supremacy theory — Chennault
need fighter escort
Air Corps Tactical School — prewar doctrine

UNESCORTED DAYLIGHT PRECISION bombing. Target priorities: submarine factories/docks/ports first, then aircraft factories and munitions, then communications and transportation. Combat proved it unworkable without long-range escort.
B-17s
dropped bombs on Japanese ships
B-25s
came below to skip 500lb bombs into sides of ships
B-29 Superfortress

Strategic bomber against Japan; first with pressurized crew compartments. Flew the 9-10 March 1945 Tokyo incendiary raid — the most destructive air raid in history, 83,000+ killed. Enola Gay (a B-29) dropped the Hiroshima bomb 6 Aug 1945.
Mitchell (airpower)
airpower offensive, spate from army, if you control air you can't be beaten; control, offense, into heart
WAFS + WFTD
(Women's Auxiliary Ferrying Sqd.) + (Women's Flying Training Detachment) = Women's AF Service Pilots
Airpower dominant role in war — Europe
centralized control, air superiority was first priority; new technology added to original doctrine (ie fighters) flexibility
WAFS personnel — military or civilian?
CIVIL SERVICE EMPLOYEES, not military members. WAFS + WFTD later merged into the WASP.
What happened to the contract flying schools after Pearl Harbor?
They INCREASED their production of pilots. The CPTP became the CAA War Training Service, training over 300,000 pilots by 1944.
Which country was NOT an Allied power?
Hungary — it was aligned with the Axis. The major Allies: US, Britain, France, USSR.
How was the German Air Force revived after WWI?
Under the guise of COMMERCIAL aviation. The Luftwaffe was officially formed 1935.
Which nation had the best prepared air force at the start of WWII?
GERMANY. Not France — France had spent on ground defense, notably the Maginot Line.
Did the Maginot Line stop Blitzkrieg?
No. Poland fell in 20 days, France in about six weeks.
Germany invades Russia — date
Which island did the Germans capture with glider-borne and parachute troops, 1941?
Crete.
Combined Bomber Offensive — target priorities in order
1st: SUBMARINE factories, docks and ports. 2nd: aircraft factories and munitions. 3rd: communications and transportation. (Aircraft factories were second, not first.)
Discriminate the airpower theorists

DOUHET — massive first strike, then the population. TRENCHARD — father of the RAF, long-range bombing of vital centers, 2/3 bomber 1/3 fighter. MITCHELL — destroy the will to resist, 20% bomber / 20% attack / 60% fighter. CHENNAULT — the bomber cannot get through without ESCORT; he was ignored.
Air Corps Tactical School doctrine
Unescorted, daylight, PRECISION bombing. It did not work; the P-51 Mustang finally solved the escort problem.
Normandy — what did Allied aircraft do beforehand?
For two months prior, bombed within a 130-mile RADIUS of the beaches. The invasion itself was almost UNOPPOSED by the Luftwaffe.
Coral Sea and Midway — significance
American VICTORIES, fought entirely by aircraft without the surface fleets sighting each other. Japan lost over 100 of its best pilots.
Was pinpoint strategic bombing used against Japan?
No — high-altitude daylight precision did not work, so the campaign shifted to LOW-LEVEL NIGHT INCENDIARY attacks.
Tokyo raid — date and casualties
9-10 March 1945. Over 83,000 killed, over 100,000 injured. Most destructive air raid in history.
Atomic bombs — the three dates
6 August 1945 Hiroshima (Enola Gay). 9 August Nagasaki. 2 September official surrender. HIROSHIMA was first.
Japanese vs Allied strength in the Pacific at the outset
Japan: 2,400,000 men plus 3,000,000 reserves, 7,500 aircraft, 400 more per month. Allies: 550,000 poorly equipped troops, 1,000 obsolete aircraft, 90 ships.
What won World War II?
The technological and wartime production capabilities of the Allied powers. The AIRCRAFT CARRIER became the dominant naval weapon.
WWII casualties
About 20 million killed, 60 million injured or disabled.
What is 'combined arms', and what made it work?

Tanks and wheeled cannons — MOBILE ARTILLERY — running right through enemy lines, combined with the airplane. Armed forts were BY-PASSED, encircled and cut off from supplies. Airplanes spotted strongholds so the army could avoid them.
Blitzkrieg — the Luftwaffe's sequence of attack

FIRST destroy any opposing air force, usually by catching it ON THE GROUND in a surprise strike. THEN hit railroads, ammunition dumps and troop concentrations unopposed, while armored divisions struck through defensive lines.
How large was Poland's army, and how quickly did it fall?
The FIFTH LARGEST in Europe — defeated in about 20 days.
Italian air power before World War II

The Italian Air Force became OBSOLETE after World War I. When MUSSOLINI came to power in 1922 he began rebuilding it — from about 100 AIRCRAFT up to about 2,600 by the time Italy entered World War II.
Where did Italy gain combat experience before World War II?
The SPANISH CIVIL WAR (from July 1936, aiding Franco's Nationalists alongside Germany) and against ETHIOPIA in 1935-1936. The Italians were battle tested and ready.
Why was the Spanish Civil War important to Germany and Italy?

Both provided aid to Franco's Nationalists and used the war to TEST THEIR ARMIES AND MILITARY TACTICS. It was a proving ground for Luftwaffe pilots and for many German aircraft later used in World War II.

sections.name: Ch 5 — Aviation: From the Cold War to Desert Storm  —  5 of 60 exam questions
cards: Cold War
antagonistic relationship as US/Russia tried to spread influence w/o wanting to go to war (we reduced military, certain the Atomic Bomb would provide all the security we needed)
Messerschmitt ME-262A
most famous jet of WWII (twin engine German jet)
Vengeance Weapons
V-1, 26ft unmanned flying bomb, “buzz bomb”; V-2 ballistic missile, rocket propelled
Berlin Airlift
Allies (US, Britain, France) flew supplies over blockade
Viet Minh — who were they?
Communist separatists in Vietnam, fighting French colonial rule. In 1950 Vietnam was a FRENCH colony.
Vietnam War
8/7/1964 Tonkin Gulf Resolution to prevent further aggression
ROLLING THUNDER
raise moral of S Vietnamese and tell N that if they didn't negotiate, bombing would continue Carried out by B-52 & F-105; F-4 beat back MiGs
Guerrilla Warfare
hit and run, disappearing into jungle
Tet Offensive
large scale surprise conventional attack on US/SV; simultaneous attacks all over SV
LINEBACKER
B-52 by Nixon; bombing NV to negotiate and cut off NV from China and Soviets (harbors, rails, SAM target)
LINEBACKER II
after failed negotiations, wanted to drive NV back again, more bombing
DESERT SHIELD
military to defend Saudi Arabia from Iraq (F-16, F-15E, F-117, A-10, KC-135, KC-10)
Civil Reserve Air Fleet
activated for Desert Shield, commercial aircraft to airlift
DESERT STORM
deter Iraq aggression, defend Saudi Arabia (military planners developed plans, as learned from Vietnam) expel Iraq from Kuwait
ALLIED FORCE
N. Atlantic Treaty Org's opposition to aggression; deter Milosevic from escalating attacks on civilians; damage Serbia's war capability
USAF
National Security Act, July 26, 1947; mission, deterrence
Sound Barrier

(Mach is speed of sound, so Mach 3 is three times speed of sound) X-1 built to explore problems of high speed flight (vibrations, control reversals, break apart) Oct 14, 1947 Chuck Yeager penetrated sound barrier with X-1 X-2 built to study heating at Mach 3
Strategic Air Command (SAC)
Defend US from nuclear attack (B-52, KC-135)
Final Coalition Air Campaign
Target Iraq's C&C, war making, etc; air defenses; supply lines&troops; give air support
in 1948, biggest bomber; 10,000lbs bombs 10,000mi
three and a half tons of cargo for Berlin Airlift

Korean War, used above enemies to strafe and cut supply (also F-51 and F-84)
DC-4
surplus made it popular, but then Constellation became the best

first turboprop airliner
Convair
short-medium range, later equipped w/ turboprop; 240 enlarged to be 44seat 340, to 56seat 440
B-52 (people/aircraft)
needed larger, longer range bomber than B-47
Northrop SM-62 Snark
Jet-PROPELLED, tailless, pilotless aircraft — an early cruise missile using INERTIAL and STELLAR guidance.
GAM 63 Rascal
small rocket propped winged bomb These allowed soldiers to stay further away from target
Navy fighter-bomber, all weather capable, Vietnam
radar and surveillance; used to alert AF/Navy for MiGs
F-105 (AF), A-7E (Navy)
attacked SAMs
C-130 — role in Vietnam
Moved men and supplies, notably during the Tet Offensive.
Best weapons in Korea
new rockets delivered by planes; bomb like Gen. Kenney's, "firebomb"
Rolling Thunder (control)
hand behind back, certain off limits, president chose targets, etc.
Linebacker (control)
military leaders planned, cut off external supply, stopped communist advance
100hr War
escaping forces caught by air power and pummeled
Who designed the first turbojet engine, and when?
Frank Whittle, 1937. But Germany flew the first jet (1939); Britain not until 1941; the US flew its first jet 1942 and fielded its first jet fighter, the F-80 Shooting Star, in 1944.
Did the US lead the world in jet propulsion during WWII?
No — GERMANY did.
Me-262 production vs use
About 1,400 produced; only about 100 actually used as FIGHTERS, a couple hundred more as fighter-bombers. Germany might have changed the war had she used more as fighters.
V-1 specifications
About 26 feet long, 3,000 lbs total, carrying 1,800 lbs of explosives. Noisy and inaccurate — the 'buzz bomb'. The V-2 was the rocket-propelled BALLISTIC missile.
The two German vengeance weapons
V-1 and V-2. (NOT the R-4 — that is the Sikorsky helicopter.)
Sikorsky R-4 — first combat rescue
April 1944, rescuing a downed pilot behind enemy lines. About 400 used. The helicopter joined in WWII but the KOREAN War really demonstrated its value.
US military manpower after WWII
From over 2 million to under 900,000, then to about 300,000. The US reduced forces because it was the only country with the atomic bomb and felt secure.
USAF primary mission on becoming a separate service, 1947
NUCLEAR DETERRENCE. National Security Act, 26 July 1947.
Berlin Airlift — cause and peak day
The Soviet Union prevented all surface transportation in or out of the city. Peak: 12,940 tons in 1,398 flights in a single day. Lasted about a year.
Who invaded South Korea?
NORTH KOREAN troops (not communist Chinese). Border: the 38th parallel.
Korean War — the lesson
The atomic arsenal ALONE was not enough to prevent involvement in war. Doctrine that emerged: centralized control, decentralized execution.
Why did American pilots beat the MiGs in Korea?
BETTER TRAINING. The MiG-15 was slightly better than the F-86, yet the exchange ratio was about nine MiGs for every one US aircraft lost.
Chuck Yeager — speed and altitude
670 mph at 42,000 feet, 14 October 1947, in the Bell X-1 (dropped from a B-29; six were built). The X-2 was built to study heating at Mach 3.
Who first reached Mach 2, in what aircraft, and when?
SCOTT CROSSFIELD, November 1953, more than 1,320 mph — in the Navy DOUGLAS D-558-II SKYROCKET (not the X-1, though he had flown it). MEL APT attained Mach 3 in the BELL X-2 in 1956.
Discriminate the X-1 and the X-2

X-1 — first aircraft credited with breaking the SOUND BARRIER: Chuck Yeager, 14 October 1947, 670 mph at 42,000 ft. X-2 — Mel Apt attained MACH 3 in 1956, but the aircraft came apart due to INERTIAL COUPLING.
Which aircraft had the laminar-flow wing?
The P-51 Mustang.
First VTOL aircraft
The Flying Bedstead.
World's first production supersonic fighter
The F-100 Super Sabre, 1953. (Not the F-101.)
Discriminate the XB-47 and the B-52
XB-47 — first all-jet bomber, but range only about 3,000 miles. B-52 — built to SUPERSEDE it, twice the size, 10,000-mile range, still in use today.
First turboprop airliner vs first pure jet airliner
Vickers Viscount — first TURBOPROP. DeHavilland Comet 1 — first PURE JET, 500 mph at 25,000-30,000 ft. Both BRITISH, not French.
DC-4 vs Constellation
The DC-4 was initially more popular because the Army had built more of them. The Constellation had two advantages: it was PRESSURIZED and about 100 mph FASTER.
Big three in general aviation manufacturing, late 1940s
Cessna, Piper and Beech. (Not Lockheed.)
US commercial air passengers — 1945, 1950, 1958
3 million, 17 million, 30 million.
Vietnam in 1950 — political status
A FRENCH colony. Truman sent a 342-member Military Assistance Advisor Group and $15 million in aid.
Which conflict is known as the helicopter war?
Vietnam.
Discriminate ROLLING THUNDER and LINEBACKER

ROLLING THUNDER — 3 years, the PRESIDENT picked the targets. LINEBACKER — Nixon, MILITARY commanders picked targets, conducted without as much worry about Chinese and Soviet reaction. LINEBACKER II lasted 12 days.
What finally destroyed the Thanh Hoa Bridge?
Smart bombs / laser-guided precision munitions.
V-22 and AV-8 — what class?
VERTICAL takeoff aircraft.
Iraq invades Kuwait — the sequence

2 August 1990, over a dispute concerning OIL and outstanding Iraqi LOANS. The Emir fled and Iraq was in complete control by 4 August. King Fahd asked the Kingdom's allies for defensive assistance on 6 August. The UN passed RESOLUTION 660 demanding Iraqi withdrawal.
Instant Thunder — the four phases in order
1. Command and control. 2. Air defenses. 3. Supply lines and troops in Kuwait. 4. Close air support.
What was activated for the first time in US history during DESERT STORM?
The Civil Reserve Air Fleet (CRAF), for logistical support. The C-5 and C-141 were key airlift links.
100-Hour War — coalition casualties
95 killed, 368 wounded, 20 missing. Iraqi losses estimated 30,000-60,000 killed.
AAA — what is it?
ANTI-AIRCRAFT ARTILLERY. Soviet-built, used with SAMs (surface-to-air missiles) against US aircraft over North Vietnam.
SAM
Surface to air missile
Tomahawk Land Attack Cruise Missiles
naval launched against Iraq
Iraq's timeline in Kuwait — the three August dates
2 AUGUST 1990: Iraq invades over oil and loan disputes. 4 AUGUST: Iraq in complete control; the Emir has fled. 6 AUGUST: King Fahd asks allies for defensive assistance, beginning DESERT SHIELD.
Which UN resolution demanded Iraqi withdrawal from Kuwait?
RESOLUTION 660.
Tet Offensive — the military result

A US/South Vietnamese victory. North Vietnamese communists lost over 50,000 in the Tet battles and were turned back out of South Vietnam. At Khe Sanh some 6,000 surrounded US Marines won, with over 10,000 communist troops killed.
Tet Offensive — the political result

It CHANGED THE POLITICAL AND SOCIAL CLIMATE in the United States. Tet was brought into American living rooms by TELEVISION nightly. Over 500,000 Americans were fighting an undeclared war, dying in a conflict the public was told was being won.
Air power at Khe Sanh — the numbers
Roughly 24,000 sorties dropped over 110,000 TONS of bombs on the enemy, and Air Force cargo planes air-dropped over 12,000 TONS of supplies into Khe Sanh under constant fire.
Iraq's counterattack into Saudi Arabia — what happened?

On 29 JANUARY Iraq launched a two-pronged attack — through the Kuwait Wafra Forest and through the Saudi border town of KHAFJI — hoping to inflict US casualties and erode American support at home. Surprise was lost when US Air Force E-8 JSTARS aircraft spotted the Iraqi tanks moving toward the border, and Marines spotted their night move from three miles away.
How was air superiority won in Desert Storm, and what did it enable?

Command and control centers were reduced to rubble; within hours key Iraqi airfields were cratered and nuclear, biological and chemical storage sites rendered unusable. With no command and control, the IRAQI AIR FORCE CEASED FLYING. Air superiority won, the battlefield was prepared for the GROUND CAMPAIGN.

stealth aircraft, invisible to enemy radar

revolutionized commercial aviation industry 1960's jets travel reached peak

Stealth, supersonic, multirole, Joint Strike Fighter
X-15 — program goals vs records actually set

GOALS: 4,500 mph and 250,000 ft (at which the airframe would reach 1,200°F). RECORDS: William Knight reached 4,520 mph, MACH 6.7, October 1967 (Flight 188) — highest speed by a manned powered aircraft. Joe Walker reached 67.0 MILES altitude, 22 August 1963 (Flight 91).
X-15 — specs, launch, and program totals

50 ft long, 22-ft wingspan, about 33,000 lbs of which over 18,000 was fuel. Built of the nickel-steel alloy INCONEL X. ROCKET powered, dropped from a modified B-52. First powered flight September 1959 at almost 1,400 mph. TWELVE pilots flew 199 flights in the THREE X-15s built; EIGHT qualified for astronaut wings by exceeding 50 miles.
What was the X-15 built from?
A nickel-steel alloy called INCONEL X.
Who flew the first eight X-15 flights?
SCOTT CROSSFIELD, the North American test pilot. Because of the speeds and altitudes he attained, many aviation historians consider him America's first astronaut.
Discriminate the X-15 and the XB-70
X-15 — rocket-powered research aircraft, built of Inconel X. XB-70 — designed as a BOMBER, supersonic B-52 replacement, 2,000 mph at 70,000 ft, first flight 1964, cancelled.
Match the wing demonstrators
X-29A → FORWARD-SWEPT wings. AD-1 Scissors → OBLIQUE wings. X-53 → MISSION-ADAPTIVE wings. Winglets → increase EFFECTIVE WINGSPAN.
What do composite materials in airframes consist of?
Nonmetallic EPOXY GRAPHITE — super-strong, lightweight, stronger than many common metals used in aircraft construction.
First twin-engine general aviation aircraft
The Beechcraft Twin Bonanza.
First turbojet business and executive aircraft
The British Hawker Siddeley 125.
Boeing 707 — year and military designation
Unveiled 1954; became the Air Force C-135. It revolutionized commercial aviation.
Which jet is described as the most successful ever built?
The Boeing 727 (1963). Not the 737.
Douglas entry into the jet-powered SHORT-HAUL market
The DC-9. (The DC-4 was a piston airliner; the DC-8 was the long-haul jet; the DC-10 was the jumbo.)
The three jumbo jets and their year
1966: Boeing 747, Lockheed L-1011, Douglas DC-10. The FIRST jumbo jet was Boeing's 747, not Douglas's DC-10.
Concorde — builders, agreement year, service
British Aircraft Corporation and Sud-Aviation; agreement 1962; began flying London/Paris to Washington DC in 1976, crossings under four hours.
TU-144 vs Concorde vs Model 2707
TU-144 — SOVIET supersonic transport. Concorde — Anglo-French. Model 2707 — the US SST, CANCELLED.
A-320 — significance
Advanced-technology airliner using composite materials for the majority of its primary structures.
Which aircraft are stealth?
B-2 and F-117A (and the B-1B is a low-altitude penetration bomber). The B-52 is NOT stealth.
U-2 and SR-71 — role
High-altitude reconnaissance.
General aviation growth, 1958-1982
GA grew FASTER than either military or commercial aviation in the US — generally not true elsewhere in the world.
Gen.A in US
geography, expense, freedom to fly
Composite materials
Nonmetallic EPOXY GRAPHITE — super-strong yet lightweight, stronger than many common metals used in aircraft construction.
Forward-swept wing
Reduces weight, cost and DRAG — but must be built STRONGER to withstand high-speed flight. Demonstrated by the X-29A.
Oblique wing aircraft
A single wing that PIVOTS to different angles across the fuselage to achieve optimum lift at different speeds. Demonstrated by the AD-1 Scissors.
Winglets
Near-vertical surfaces at the WINGTIPS. They reduce the wingtip VORTICES that cause induced drag, increasing the wing's EFFECTIVE SPAN and efficiency.
Mission-adaptive wings
Change shape IN FLIGHT for best efficiency — forward for slow flight, backward for supersonic. Demonstrated by the X-53.
Canards
horizontal surfaces forward of main wings for trim/control; increases maneuverability (& wings can be smaller)
UAV
Unmanned Aerial Vehicle
Hypersonic transports
designed to fly at Mach 5 or higher
Modular air vehicle
build vehicle from different sections, allowing it to do different missions; mix and match for needs
Waverider
hyper or super sonic vehicle with attached shock wave along leading edge; appears to ride own shock wave
Who set the X-15 speed record, and what was it?
William Knight, October 1967, Flight 188 — 4,520 mph, MACH 6.7. The highest speed reached by a manned, powered aircraft.
Who set the X-15 altitude record, and what was it?
Joe Walker, 22 August 1963, Flight 91 — 67.0 MILES. The highest altitude ever reached by a powered manned aircraft.
X-15 program — pilots, flights, aircraft built
TWELVE pilots flew 199 flights in the THREE X-15s built. EIGHT qualified for USAF or NASA astronaut wings by exceeding 50 miles. One, NEIL ARMSTRONG, commanded the first lunar landing.

sections.name: Ch 7 — Basic Aeronautics and Aerodynamics  —  3 of 60 exam questions
cards: Mach number

The ratio of an object's speed to the speed of sound in air. Mach 3 = three times the speed of sound. The speed of sound DECREASES as altitude increases (it tracks temperature). Ernst Mach determined the correct value.
Airfoil — definition
Any surface designed to obtain a useful DYNAMIC REACTION from the air through which it moves — producing lift. Its parts: leading edge, camber, trailing edge, chord.
Relative Wind
opposite flight path, impacts airfoil at any angle to chord line
Angle of Attack
angle of chord line and oncoming relative wind (Angle of Incidence: between chord and centerline)
Bernoulli's principle
as the velocity of a fluid increases, pressure decreases (pressure top less than below, move up)
Streamlines
flow of air over an airfoil
Four forces of flight
lift, drag, thrust, weight
Vector
mathematical illustration showing direction and magnitude (like velocity)
Stall — what physically happens?
The streamlines of air next to the wing SEPARATE from the airfoil surface. The low-pressure region over the wing is lost, lift is destroyed, and weight takes over.
Weight distribution
where useful load is has profound effect; rotates around center of gravity in direction of weight
Thrust vectoring
allows thrust to be pointed in any direction to assist in maneuvering 9pointed along a direction other than longitudinal axis; exhaust plates, port, etc.)
Shock Wave
outspeeding pressure wave, air is forced aside abruptly by plane; Types: Compression (air moves aside at leading edge) and Expansion (filling in as air passes)
Airfoil — Leading edge
meets wind first, slower thicker
Airfoil — Trailing edge
they meet again
Airfoil — Chord
imaginary line, leading to trailing edge
Improve — Lift
increase camber, or angle of attack
Improve — Weight
lighter, composite materials
Improve — Drag
parallel to relative wind: reduce friction
Drag — Wave
when flowing across a shock wave, temp, pressure, velocity change – the drag a result of lost energy
Standard sea-level pressure
14.7 psi, or 29.92 inches of mercury.
Standard temperature lapse rate — and a worked example
3.5 degrees F per 1,000 feet. If it is 92F at the beach, a pilot at 8,000 ft reads 92 - (3.5 x 8) = 92 - 28 = 64 degrees F.
Discriminate: aeronautics vs aerodynamics
AERONAUTICS — the movement of objects through the atmosphere. AERODYNAMICS — the science relating to the ENERGY OF AIR IN MOTION.
Discriminate: induced lift vs dynamic lift

INDUCED LIFT comes from the LOW-pressure air on TOP of the wing (produced by camber). DYNAMIC LIFT comes from the HIGH-pressure air on the BOTTOM. Increasing ANGLE OF ATTACK gains you BOTH — which is why lift rises sharply with angle of attack.
Name the four parts of an airfoil

Leading edge (meets the air first), camber (determines thickness and thus lift), trailing edge (rear junction of upper and lower surfaces), chord (the imaginary line, the starting point for designing the cross-section).
Is air a fluid with viscosity?
YES. All fluids possess viscosity, and air is included. Slowing the flow rate is called viscous drag.
Are laminar and turbulent flow found at the same place on an aircraft?
No — they are found at DIFFERENT locations. Laminar is the smooth and more desirable pattern.
Name the four types of drag
FRICTION (air rubbing the surface — like sandpaper). FORM (shape creating turbulence). INDUCED (the wingtip vortex tilting the lift vector rearward). WAVE (energy lost across a shock wave).
What happens to lift as air gets less dense?
Less lift is available.
Gross weight vs useful load
GROSS WEIGHT is the total weight limitation. USEFUL LOAD = maximum gross weight minus empty weight.
Turbulence
churning of air
Improve — Thrust
propels aircraft forward: engine, much power little weight
Drag — Friction
friction of air against parts of plane (like rubbing sandpaper)
Drag — Form
shape creates turbulence
WHY does a wing generate lift? (explain the mechanism)

Camber makes air travel faster over the upper surface; by Bernoulli, faster flow means LOWER PRESSURE there — that is INDUCED lift. Higher pressure beneath the wing pushes up — that is DYNAMIC lift. Increasing angle of attack increases BOTH.
WHY does a stall happen, and why is it not simply about being slow?

A stall is defined by airflow SEPARATION, not airspeed. Past the critical angle of attack the streamlines can no longer follow the upper surface — they separate, the low-pressure region collapses, and lift is lost. An aircraft can stall at ANY airspeed if the angle of attack is exceeded.
WHY does the speed of sound decrease with altitude?

The speed of sound depends on air TEMPERATURE, not pressure or density. Temperature falls with altitude through the troposphere, so the speed of sound falls with it. This is why the same true airspeed produces a higher Mach number at altitude.
WHY does less dense air reduce lift and engine performance?

Lift depends on the MASS of air the wing deflects. Thinner air means fewer molecules moving over the wing per second, so less lift for the same speed and angle. Engines suffer for the same reason — less oxygen mass entering per second.
WHY does induced drag exist at all? (trace the chain)

High pressure under the wing spills around the tip into the low pressure above, creating a VORTEX. The vortex tilts the local lift vector rearward, and the rearward component IS induced drag. Winglets attack the vortex, which is why they reduce this specific drag.
WHY is a shock wave a source of drag?

Above Mach 1 the aircraft outruns its own pressure wave, so air is forced aside abruptly instead of flowing smoothly. Crossing the shock, pressure, temperature and velocity all change sharply — and the energy lost in that change is WAVE DRAG.
How do aluminum and composites address the force of WEIGHT?

Weight directly opposes lift, so the airplane must be built of the LIGHTEST-WEIGHT materials usable. Most airplanes today are built of ALUMINUM ALLOYS, used for their STRENGTH AND LIGHT WEIGHT. COMPOSITES are used more and more — they shape easily and some have strength EXCEEDING METALS.

sections.name: Ch 8 — Aircraft in Motion  —  6 of 60 exam questions
cards: Turboprop — the one-line definition
A gas TURBINE fastened to a PROPELLER. It produces about twice the power of a reciprocating engine.
Pure jet (turbojet) — where does the thrust come from?
ENTIRELY from the jet EXHAUST — no propeller and no bypass fan contribution.
Name the major parts of an airplane
FUSELAGE, WING (with ailerons), ENGINE, and TAIL or EMPENNAGE — which comprises the HORIZONTAL STABILIZER with ELEVATOR, and the VERTICAL STABILIZER with RUDDER.
Vertical axis / Rudder
Yaw
Lateral axis / Elevator
Pitch
Engines — Reciprocating
four stroke, five event, circular motion, in cylinder, fuel into energy
Engines — Turbine
whirl, refers to device having vanes where wheel turns as vanes struck by moving fluid; take in air, accelerate, push through exhaust
TurboFan
one or more compressor blades, more air pulled in; large amount air accelerate less to get high thrust
Fuselage — Truss
tubing welded to make well braced framework
Fuselage — Monocoque
covering of skin to provide strength (almost like circles as base, then skin covering)
Fuselage — SemiMonocoque
internal braces to help skin carry force; longitudinal stringers, blukheads
Landing Gear — Conventional
two wheels forward, one at tail
Landing Gear — Tricycle
one front, two behind, nose gear linked to rudder
Landing Gear — Tandem
one in front of second on fuselage, outrigger wheels needed
Systems — Hydraulic
brakes, landing gear, flight controls, flaps; pressurized fluid to make parts move, how you can press brakes to stop so many tons
Mechanical (instruments)
gear, float, gyro (Gyro Stability: spinning flat weight lines up in one of its axis, perpendicular to weight)
Pressure (instruments)
principle that fluid exerts pressure, and it decreases with height; ie, indicates altitude
Electrical (instruments)
operates on electricity and magnetism, being used more and more
Use classification — Performance
tells how craft responded to commands
Use classification — Control
tells state of devices
Engine (instruments)
tells how thrust producing device is operating (rpm, oil, fluid flow)
Tachometer
speed measure, how fast engine crankshaft is turning (rpm)
Oil pressure and temperature
oil while engine's operating
Airspeed Indicator
speed through air mph or knots
Altimeter
aneroid barometer, altitude in feet (pressure of mercury)
Turn-and-slip indicator

Two-in-one instrument. NEEDLE = direction AND RATE of turn. BALL in the curved glass tube (the inclinometer) = QUALITY of the turn. Keep both straight; collapsing them into one phrase is how the question gets missed.
Vertical velocity indicator
Shows RATE of climb or DESCENT, in FEET PER MINUTE. Also called the rate-of-climb or vertical speed indicator.
The three axes — name, path, control surface, motion
LONGITUDINAL: nose to tail; AILERONS; ROLL. LATERAL: wingtip through fuselage to wingtip; ELEVATOR; PITCH. VERTICAL: bottom of fuselage through the top; RUDDER; YAW.
Four strokes of a reciprocating engine, in order
Intake, compression, power, exhaust. (Five events — ignition occurs near the top of compression.) The CYLINDER converts fuel into energy; the PROPELLER converts that energy into thrust.
Match the engine to its description — turbojet
Air accelerated and compressed by STATOR and ROTOR blades, then mixed with fuel and ignited in the combustion section, producing high-velocity gas.
Match the engine to its description — turbofan
Produces GREATER thrust and is MORE FUEL EFFICIENT than a standard turbojet; pulls in much more air, quieter.
Match the engine to its description — propfan
Combines the AIR-MOVING efficiency of the turbofan with the THRUSTING efficiency of a propeller. Resembles a ship's screw.
Match the engine to its description — ramjet/scramjet
Must be traveling through the air very fast to work; no moving parts. In a SCRAMJET the incoming air is NOT slowed to subsonic before combustion.
Turboprop — power comparison
A gas turbine driving a propeller produces about TWICE the power of a reciprocating engine.
Flaps, slats, spoilers, drag devices — discriminate

FLAP: increases the CAMBER of the wing where attached; used for takeoff and landing. SLAT: protrusion from the LEADING edge producing a SLOT; adds to INDUCED lift. SPOILER: destroys the LAMINAR flow and reduces induced lift. DRAG DEVICE: produces drag WITHOUT affecting lift.
Three fuselage types — discriminate
TRUSS: longerons and struts welded together at various angles. MONOCOQUE: the COVERING alone provides the strength. SEMIMONOCOQUE: INTERNAL BRACES help the skin carry the stresses.
Three landing gear types — discriminate
CONVENTIONAL: two main FRONT wheels plus a small TAILWHEEL. TRICYCLE: a NOSEWHEEL plus two main wheels. TANDEM: two sets of main wheels one BEHIND the other, requiring outriggers.
Why do most small aircraft lack retractable gear?
Cost and weight. Retractable gear reduces drag; fixed gear is cheaper and simpler.
What law is the hydraulic system based on?
PASCAL'S LAW — pressure applied to a liquid in a closed container. It operates brakes, flaps, propeller pitch AND the landing gear.
What does a generator do on an aircraft?
Charges the battery and powers electrical devices and controls — engine start, radios, navigation and landing lights. It does NOT ignite the fuel-air mixture.
Two ways of classifying instruments
By USE: engine, flight, navigation. By PRINCIPLE OF OPERATION: mechanical, pressure, electrical. (A third split is performance vs control.)
One of aviation's first fuel gauges used what three things?
String, a stick, and a CORK. Early airspeed indicators were merely wind gauges.
Match: measures altitude, usually an aneroid barometer
Altimeter — calibrated in inches of mercury.
Match: heavy rotor wheel mounted free to rotate
Gyroscope.
Match: compass using a gyroscopic device, little affected by turbulence
Heading indicator.
Match: the most basic and important navigational instrument
Magnetic compass.
Match: gyroscopic instrument giving a horizon for pitch and bank
Attitude indicator (artificial horizon).
Match: informs the pilot of speed through the air using a pitot tube
Airspeed indicator.
What does 'fuselage' literally mean?
To shape like a spindle; to streamline. ('Hydraulic' means water tube.)
Tilt-rotor aircraft
Turn the rotors up to take off and land like a helicopter, then down to fly like a fixed-wing aircraft.
Name the major parts of an aircraft
FUSELAGE, WING, TAIL (empennage), HORIZONTAL STABILIZER, VERTICAL STABILIZER — plus engine and landing gear.
What is the empennage?
The TAIL assembly — horizontal stabilizer, vertical stabilizer, elevator and rudder.
Name the three MAJOR flight control surfaces
AILERONS (roll), ELEVATOR (pitch), RUDDER (yaw).
Name the OTHER flight control surfaces
Flaps, slats, spoilers and drag devices.
What is the purpose of anti-skid brakes?
To prevent the wheels from LOCKING and SKIDDING during braking.
Fuel system — what does the fuel pump do?
Delivers fuel to the engine under pressure in a FORCE-FEED system, where gravity feed is not used.
Fuel system — what does the vent pipe do?
Allows air into the tank as fuel is drawn out, preventing a vacuum that would stop fuel flow.
Fuel system — what does the fuel strainer do?
Filters contaminants and water out of the fuel before it reaches the engine.
Fuel system — what does the fuel tank drain do?
Allows water and sediment collected at the low point of the tank to be drained off before flight.
Fuel system — what does the cockpit fuel selector do?
Lets the pilot choose which tank feeds the engine, or shut fuel off entirely.
What is gyroscopic stability?
A spinning flat weight resists changes to the orientation of its spin axis — it stays lined up on one of its axes. This is what makes gyro instruments work.
Performance vs control instruments
PERFORMANCE instruments tell how the aircraft RESPONDED to a command. CONTROL instruments tell the STATE of the devices.
Name the engine instruments
Tachometer (crankshaft rpm), oil pressure, oil temperature.
Name the flight instruments
Airspeed indicator, altimeter, turn-and-slip indicator, vertical velocity indicator, attitude indicator. They tell altitude, airspeed and attitude, and how well the craft is being controlled.
Name the navigation instruments
Magnetic compass, heading indicator, clock, airspeed indicator — plus radio, radar and GPS. They get the aircraft from departure to destination.
What did early pilots use a string on the aircraft for?
To determine SLIP — whether the aircraft was flying coordinated. Early fuel gauges used string, a stick and a cork; early airspeed indicators were wind gauges.
What is the inclinometer?
The BALL in the curved glass tube of the turn-and-slip indicator. It shows the QUALITY of the turn (coordinated or not).
What does the clock do among navigation instruments?
Measures the passage of TIME — essential for dead reckoning, where time, heading and speed give position.
Rotor blades vs stator blades in a turbojet
ROTOR blades gather air and push it backward; STATOR blades straighten the flow. Together they accelerate and compress the air before the combustion section.
What happens in the combustion section of a turbojet?
Compressed air is mixed with fuel and IGNITED, producing high-velocity gas that strikes the turbine — which spins and drives the compressor.
V/STOL — what does it mean?
Vertical / Short TakeOff and Landing. Rotors turn up to take off like a helicopter, then back to fixed-wing flight.
What is a waverider?
A hypersonic or supersonic vehicle with a shock wave attached along its leading edge — it appears to ride its own shock wave.
Hypersonic transport — what speed?
Designed to fly at MACH 5 or higher.
Fixed vs retractable landing gear — the tradeoff
FIXED is cheaper and simpler. RETRACTABLE reduces DRAG. Most small aircraft use fixed gear because of cost and weight.
Which two purposes are flaps often used for?
TAKEOFF and LANDING — they increase both lift and drag.
Where are drag devices mounted?
On trailing edges or on the fuselage. Speed brakes, air brakes and parachutes are examples.
What is thrust vectoring?
Directing engine thrust along an axis OTHER than the longitudinal axis, to assist maneuvering — using exhaust plates, ports and similar devices.
Why is the propeller called the action end of the engine?
Because it CONVERTS the engine's useful energy into THRUST as it spins.
What is a monocoque fuselage made from?
A stressed SKIN covering that provides all the required strength by itself — no internal bracing carrying the load.
Systems — Electrical
generator provides charge, for engine, radio, lights, etc.
WHY does a turbofan produce more thrust and better fuel economy than a turbojet?

Thrust equals mass of air moved times how much it is accelerated. A turbofan moves a LARGE mass of air and accelerates it a LITTLE; a turbojet moves a small mass and accelerates it a lot. Moving more air gently is more efficient and quieter than moving little air violently.
WHY must a ramjet already be flying fast to work?

It has NO compressor. It relies entirely on its own forward speed to ram air into the inlet and compress it. At rest there is no ram effect, so no compression, so no combustion. A scramjet is the same except the air is not slowed to subsonic first.
WHY does a spoiler destroy lift while a flap increases it?

A FLAP increases the wing's CAMBER, strengthening the pressure difference that makes lift. A SPOILER disrupts the LAMINAR flow over the upper surface, destroying the low-pressure region — the same separation that occurs in a stall, deliberately induced.
WHY does a semimonocoque fuselage exist if monocoque is simpler?

In a pure MONOCOQUE the skin alone carries every load, so it must be thick and heavy, and any dent is structural. SEMIMONOCOQUE adds stringers and bulkheads so the skin SHARES the load — lighter overall and far more damage-tolerant.
WHY does the hydraulic system let a pilot stop many tons of aircraft with one foot?

Pascal's law: pressure applied to a confined liquid is transmitted undiminished throughout it. A small force on a small piston becomes a large force on a large piston — mechanical advantage. This is why hydraulics also move gear, flaps and controls.
WHY does a gyroscopic instrument work?

A spinning mass RESISTS changes to the orientation of its spin axis. That rigidity gives a stable reference the aircraft can be measured against — which is what makes the attitude indicator and heading indicator possible, and why they are little affected by turbulence.
Who invented the ramjet, and when?
Frenchman RENE LORIN, in 1913. It is the simplest of all jet engines because it has NO MOVING PARTS — inertia 'rams' air into a streamlined chamber.
High-bypass turbofans — what is the bypass ratio, and where are they efficient?
Bypass ratios of 60 TO 1 or greater — 60 times as much air flows AROUND the turbine core as passes through it. Very efficient at SUBSONIC speeds; for airliners about MACH 0.8, or 525 mph.
Why were propfans largely abandoned?
NOISE, COST and fluctuating FUEL PRICES. Only Ukraine currently operates a propfan aircraft — the ANTONOV AN-70.

sections.name: Ch 9 — Flight Navigation  —  5 of 60 exam questions
cards: Great Circle
circle on earth's surface passing through center; anything else is a small circle
Graticule

The basic GRID SYSTEM of latitude and longitude. 18 primary great circles run north-south (longitude); the equator plus parallel small circles run east-west (latitude), spaced 10 degrees. Numbers across the top, letters down the left.
Prime meridian
zero degrees, great circle through Greenwich, England
Meridian
north south line that's part of a great circle
Sectional Aeronautical chart
aircraft over short distance, Lambert-conformal, info to visually monitor ground
Controlled Airspace
airspace has several subdivisions, flyers subject to FAA air traffic controllers
Airways
three dimensional highways in the sky
Special use airspace
Airspace most pilots must avoid. PROHIBITED means flight is NEVER permitted. RESTRICTED means it may sometimes be entered, with permission.
True course
indicates the course the airplane will follow (w/ regard to true north, earth's north geographic pole)
True airspeed
speed of plane through air
Ground speed
How FAST the aircraft is moving across the SURFACE of the earth — true airspeed adjusted for the wind component.
Wind Triangle
used by pilot to figure out where wind drift will cause craft to fly, to counter effect drift (degrees between true course and ground track, steer that many into wind)
Aircraft radio
navigational aid, pilots link with FAA etc.
Drag — Induced
vortex causes lift vector aslant towards wing; lift vector same direction as drag vector adds to drag
Very-High-Frequency Omnidirectional Radio Range (VOR)

360 degree circle from station, select a radial, head for station. Includes plane receivers and ground station. Stationary signal and rotational signal line up north. Rotational moves around, difference converted to radial info so pilot can select route
Automatic Direction Finder (ADF)
same beacon signal, but not selectable. Needle on navigational display is used
Distance Measuring Equipment (DME)

VOR stations have special Tactical Air Navigation (TACAN); with VOR it's a VORTAC. TACAN portion will respond with broadcast signal when it receives one from DME. DME measures time it will take to go to VORTAC plane and return, converts to nautical miles
Long Range navigation (LORAN)

broadcast signals, received by slave stations, which broadcast delayed responding signals; time differences shown, plane position can be plotted on LORAN chart; displays time diff. continuously (on auto)
GPS — how many satellites must be visible for a fix?
FOUR. The receiver then gives latitude, longitude, elevation and current time. (On constellation SIZE the book is inconsistent — Ch 9 says roughly 30, Ch 26 says 24.)
GPS — why are two position signals broadcast?
Civilian users needed access to position data as well as the military, so the GPS satellites send out TWO signals for position data — one more precise for military use, one for everyone else.
Differential GPS — how does it improve accuracy?

A ground GPS station whose latitude, longitude and elevation are very precisely known broadcasts a CORRECTION signal to nearby aircraft. This fixes small errors in the satellite signal, greatly improving accuracy at that location.
Inertial Navigation System (INS)
Entirely SELF-CONTAINED — needs no external signal. ACCELEROMETERS measure movement, which a computer translates into speed, direction and distance. (Note: INERTIAL, not 'internal'.)
Area Navigation System (RNAV)

computer controlled, stations and receivers; VOR type stations or GPS as reference, allows to fly w/o following airways; start and end, monitors which VOR stations you pass, compares path to prediction
Instrument Landing System (ILS)

short distance, purpose to land plane; precise direction signals; lateral centerline, vertical glide slope; maybe outer(blue) middle(amber) inner(white) indicators; glide slope and beacon receiver, glide slope and azimuth on VOR
Microwave Landing System (MLS)
wider beams, funnel (120horizontal, 20 vertical degrees)
Unpaved (chart symbol)
magenta
Facilities, four ticks no tower (chart symbol)
magenta
Tower (chart symbol)
blue
FAA (federal Aviation Admin)
establishes and enforces restrictions in US
How many primary great circles form the lines of longitude?
EIGHTEEN, producing meridians at 10-degree spacing. Parallels of latitude are also spaced 10 degrees.
Which projection is cylindrical? Which uses a cone?
MERCATOR — cylindrical. CONIC — a cone placed over the earth. Sectionals use Lambert conformal and are the most commonly used chart.
Relief — what is it, and how is it depicted?
Relief describes ELEVATIONS. Depicted by CONTOUR LINES, COLOR TINTS and SHADING.
Chart colors — the set to know
Cities and towns: BRIGHT YELLOW. Very small towns: a small BLACK CIRCLE. Water (hydrographic): BLUE. Highways: BLACK or RED. Unpaved airport: MAGENTA. Airport with tower: BLUE.
In what order are coordinates read?
LATITUDE first, then longitude.
What is the largest area of controlled airspace?
The CONTINENTAL CONTROL AREA. It generally begins at 14,500 FEET above mean sea level, extends upward, and covers the United States (excluding Alaska and Hawaii) like a blanket.
Which airways are shown on sectional charts?
LOW-altitude airways, also known as VICTOR airways, based on VOR locations. HIGH-altitude airways are NOT defined on sectionals.
Two types of airspace marked for pilots to avoid
PROHIBITED and RESTRICTED.
What does MOA stand for and mean?
Military Operations Area — airspace where military FLIGHT-TRAINING activities are conducted. Low-level military training routes on sectionals are MTRs.
Discriminate: magnetic variation vs compass deviation
VARIATION — the magnetic poles are not at the geographic poles. DEVIATION — electrical equipment and metals in the aircraft, which is why the compass must be adjusted after installation.
Discriminate: pilotage vs dead reckoning
PILOTAGE — navigating by reference to visible LANDMARKS. DEAD RECKONING — systematic consideration of ALL factors affecting the flight.
What does the wind triangle find?
The TRUE HEADING that compensates for the effect of wind.
Discriminate: VOR vs ADF vs DME

VOR — SELECT a radial from a 360-degree array; two signals, one stationary and one rotating; does NOT compensate for wind. ADF — direction to a radio station, NOT selectable, read on a needle; no allowance for wind. DME — round-trip signal timing converted to NAUTICAL MILES.
What is a VORTAC?
A VOR co-located with a TACAN. The TACAN component replies to the DME interrogation.
LORAN — what two transmitters, and what is measured?
A MASTER station and SLAVE stations. Position comes from the TIME DIFFERENCE between their signals, plotted on a LORAN chart.
GPS constellation size — CAUTION, the book gives two numbers

Ch 9 says ROUGHLY 30 satellites, and that the total varies as satellites are repaired and upgraded. Ch 26 says a constellation of 24. Both appear in Journey of Flight. A receiver needs any FOUR in view for latitude, longitude, elevation and time.
What is unique about INS?
It is entirely SELF-CONTAINED — no external signal required. Accelerometers measure movement, translated into speed, direction and distance.
The three landing systems

ILS (lateral centerline + vertical glide slope; markers outer BLUE, middle AMBER, inner WHITE). MLS (much wider coverage, about 120 degrees horizontal and 20 vertical). Differential GPS (very accurate, allows curved paths and tiered altitudes).
Weather radar — its most important function
Showing TURBULENCE ahead of the aircraft, not just areas of precipitation.
What does a grid on a map provide, and how is it built?
A system of COORDINATES. Horizontal and vertical lines are drawn, with NUMBERS and LETTERS placed on them; any location is found by reading across and down to the point of INTERSECTION.
What is the graticule?
The basic grid system of latitude and longitude lines.
Define hemisphere
HALF OF A SPHERE. The equator divides the northern and southern hemispheres.
Parallels vs meridians — which is latitude, which is longitude?
PARALLELS run east-west and mark LATITUDE (all are small circles except the equator). MERIDIANS run north-south and mark LONGITUDE (each is half of a great circle).
How are mines shown on a sectional chart?
With crossed-pick symbols and a label — they are cultural features, charted as landmarks for navigation.
Cultural vs hydrographic features
CULTURAL = man-made (cities bright yellow, small towns as black circles, highways black or red). HYDROGRAPHIC = water, shown in BLUE.
Why is water a useful navigational aid?
A pilot can identify a lake by comparing its actual shape SEEN FROM THE AIR to the shape shown on the CHART. Water features are easy to identify and accurately drawn.
Name the ten steps of dead reckoning flight planning

Check the weather; draw the TC line; select checkpoints; estimate true airspeed; determine wind correction angle, true heading and ground speed; determine magnetic variation and magnetic heading; determine the compass heading; determine time en route; determine fuel usage; file a flight plan.
What are the four steps in preparing for pilotage navigation?
(a) Draw a course line. (b) Mark it in 10-MILE segments. (c) Select landmarks to be used. (d) Use brackets to help maintain the proper TRACK over the ground.
What are the three basic components of an INS?
Accelerometers, a stable platform (gyro-stabilized), and a computer. It gives the navigator speed, direction and distance travelled — entirely self-contained.
What are the two types of GPS landing systems?
Standard GPS approach guidance and DIFFERENTIAL GPS — the latter is far more accurate and allows curved paths and tiered altitudes.
What is a radial?
A magnetic bearing line FROM a VOR station. The pilot selects one from the 360-degree array and tracks to or from the station.
Weather radar vs ground radar
WEATHER radar shows precipitation, but its most important function is showing TURBULENCE ahead. GROUND radar bounces energy off aircraft, returning bright spots on a scope.
Three factors affecting compass deviation
Metal in the aircraft structure, electrical power and equipment, and the aircraft's own magnetic fields. The compass must be adjusted after installation.
What causes magnetic variation?
The MAGNETIC poles are not in the same place as the GEOGRAPHIC poles. Lines of equal variation are isogonic lines.
True course vs magnetic course
TRUE COURSE is measured against TRUE north (geographic pole). Apply VARIATION to get the MAGNETIC course, then DEVIATION to get the compass heading.
How is direction measured from a true course line?
Where the true course line crosses a line of longitude, direction in degrees is measured CLOCKWISE from the longitude line to the true course.
What are MTRs?
Military Training Routes — low-level military routes appearing on sectional aeronautical charts.
Prohibited vs restricted airspace
PROHIBITED — flight is NEVER permitted. RESTRICTED — may sometimes be entered, with permission. Both are clearly marked for pilots to avoid.
What is the FAA responsible for?
It is the regulatory body for ALL of aviation — it establishes and enforces restrictions in the United States. Controlled airspace is serviced by its air traffic controllers.
Joint-use airports — how are facilities handled?
Facilities are NOT necessarily shared by the military and civilians. On charts the military name appears above the civilian name.
What are the two broadest classifications of airports?
CIVIL and MILITARY / JOINT-USE.
What is a sectional chart used for?
Visual navigation over relatively SHORT distances in small aircraft — Lambert conformal projection, with enough detail to monitor the ground visually. The most commonly used chart.
Radar
reflected radio energy. Energy bounced back as bright spots, radar scope is very far
WHY is a great circle route the shortest path between two points?
A great circle's plane passes through the earth's CENTER, so its arc is the shortest possible line across a sphere's surface. Any other circle (a small circle) cuts a shallower, longer path.
WHY must a pilot apply variation AND deviation, in that order?

TRUE course is measured against the geographic pole. VARIATION corrects for the MAGNETIC pole being somewhere else, giving magnetic course. DEVIATION then corrects for metal and electrical equipment in the specific aircraft, giving the compass heading actually flown.
WHY does the wind triangle work?

The aircraft moves through an AIR MASS which is itself moving over the ground. Heading and true airspeed give one vector, wind gives another; their sum is the actual track and ground speed. Steering into the wind by the drift angle cancels the sideways component.
WHY does GPS need four satellites, not three?

Three ranges fix a point in three dimensions — but only if the receiver's clock is perfectly synchronized with the satellites'. It is not. The fourth satellite solves for the clock error as a fourth unknown, which is why GPS also gives precise TIME.
WHY is INS valuable despite drifting over time?

It is entirely SELF-CONTAINED — it cannot be jammed, blocked by terrain, or lost when out of range of a station. It measures its own acceleration and integrates. The tradeoff is accumulating error, which is why it is often paired with GPS.
WHY does a VOR give more usable information than an ADF?

An ADF needle only points AT a station — the pilot must work out position from the bearing. A VOR broadcasts a stationary and a rotating signal; their phase difference identifies WHICH of 360 radials the aircraft is on, so a specific course can be selected and tracked.
At what altitude does the continental control area begin?
Generally 14,500 FEET above mean sea level, extending upward and covering the United States except Alaska and Hawaii.
Why do pilots have to fly into control zones?
Because control zones surround MANY AIRPORTS — they are unavoidable when arriving or departing.

Taxiway

Control tower.
Match the airport facility — planes use these to get from place to place on the airport
Taxiways.

Ramp.

FBO (Fixed-Base Operation).
