Hangar.
Match the airport facility — board aircraft and retrieve baggage
Passenger terminal.
Match the airport facility — weather forecasts and flight plan assistance
Flight Service Station.
Match the airport facility — surface used to take off and land
Runway.
Controlled vs uncontrolled field
CONTROLLED = has an operating control tower. UNCONTROLLED = no operating tower.
Beacon colors — the discrimination
MILITARY field: one GREEN and TWO WHITE flashes. CIVILIAN land airport: alternating GREEN and a SINGLE WHITE.
Airport lighting colors
TAXIWAY lights: BLUE. RUNWAY EDGE lighting: WHITE.
How can a pilot adjust runway light intensity?
Tune the specified radio frequency and KEY THE MICROPHONE — the NUMBER OF TIMES it is keyed sets the intensity. To conserve electricity the lights shut off automatically after about 15 minutes.
Taxiways vs runways — width and identification
Taxiways are NARROWER than runways, and identified by a LETTER rather than a number.
Runway numbering — two worked examples
Compass heading 257 degrees → runway 26. Compass heading 033 → runway 3. Take the heading, round to the nearest ten, drop the last digit.
How are parallel runways delineated?
By adding L, C or R to the runway number.
What does ATIS stand for and do?
Automated Terminal Information System — a continuous recorded broadcast of airport and weather information, which reduces congestion near the airport.
Dangers on an airport ramp
Aircraft starting engines, taxiing aircraft, and numerous ground vehicles.
Encroachment — definition
Development building up around the airport boundary. Closely tied to noise abatement procedures.
What is the most common taxiway type, and why the name?
The PARALLEL taxiway — it parallels the runway.
What are the airport concerns and challenges?

WILDLIFE — the biggest concern; birds are the worst problem, and larger game animals are also a hazard (cattle grates and fences are used). NOISE — aircraft are not quiet near the ground. ENCROACHMENT — development building up around the airport.
How do airports manage the wildlife hazard?
CATTLE GRATES placed across roads where they pass through a fence, and FENCES to keep animals off the runway. Where that fails, animals are tranquilized and moved, or killed.

sections.name: Ch 18 — The Atmosphere  —  3 of 60 exam questions
cards: Atmosphere and Space
(no boundary) best described by AEROSPACE; atmosphere is where we don't need life support
Dew Point
air temperature at which saturation occurs; Dew Temp is temp at or below which vapor will condense
Evaporation
process by which liquid water molecules change to gas/vapor state and enter atmosphere (temp affects it)
Sublimation
water molecules leave frozen state and directly enter atmosphere w/o changing into liquid first
Humidity — absolute vs relative
ABSOLUTE humidity is the ACTUAL AMOUNT of water vapor in a volume of air. RELATIVE humidity expresses how much MORE the air can hold before saturation, as a percentage.
Insolation
rate at which earth's surface is heated by solar radiation
Convection currents along a shoreline
Heated air rises VERTICALLY (convection); the resulting horizontal flow is wind, transferred by ADVECTION. By DAY the land is warmer, so the breeze blows from SEA to LAND; at NIGHT it reverses.
Jet stream

A narrow current of high-speed air moving around the hemisphere in a wavelike pattern, near 30,000 ft. Flows generally WEST TO EAST. Shifts frequently, migrates with the seasons, and may act as a barrier between cold air north and warm air south.
Weather
the condition of the atmosphere at any particular time and place (day2day changes in atmospheric conditions)
Atmosphere (composition)
78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, argon, neon, helium, methane, hydrogen, xenon, and variable water vapor, carbon dioxide, ozone, carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen dioxide
The four ways atmospheric regions are classified (source wording)
By TEMPERATURE DISTRIBUTION; by PHYSICOCHEMICAL (physical and chemical properties) PROCESSES DISTRIBUTION; by MOLECULAR COMPOSITION; and by DYNAMIC-KINETIC (force-motion) PROCESSES.
Temp — Troposphere (and pause)
to 10mi temp decreases
Temp — Mesosphere (and pause)
to 50mi increase then decrease
Temp — Thermosphere
to 300mi increases
Physicochemical — Ozonosphere
10-30 miles. Oxygen picks up an extra atom to form ozone, which shields the surface from harmful solar radiation.
Physicochemical — Ionosphere
Roughly 25-250 miles. Atoms lose or gain electrons to form IONS. It reflects certain radio waves back toward earth.
Physicochemical — Neutrosphere
Below the ionosphere, down to the earth. Very little ionization takes place here.
Physicochemical — Chemosphere
Overlaps the ozonosphere and ionosphere. Begins at the stratopause and includes the mesosphere. Important PHOTOCHEMICAL (radiant energy plus chemical) reactions occur here.
Molecular Composition — Homosphere
to 60mi same gaseous composition
Molecular Composition — Heterosphere
up from 55-60 molecules/atoms further apart, take on vertical arrangement
Dynamic/Kinetic — Exosphere
top of heterosphere, processes occur, atmospheric particles free orbit subject only to earth's gravity
Evaporation cycle
water to vapor (solar radiation heats) to condensation (moves over cooler air to below dew point, makes fog and clouds) to precipitation
Heat Transfer — Conduction
heating by direct contact
Heat Transfer — Convection
heat transfer by vertical motion
Heat Transfer — Advection
temp transferred horizontally, wind or moving air
Heat Transfer — Radiation
heat energy of sun reaches earth as this
Fog — Radiation
night, when land radiates heat; cools air near it by conduction below dew point
Fog — Advection
wind blows moist air over cool surface, cools to dew pt temp
Fog — Evaporation
or steam; when cold air moves over warm water; normal evaporation saturates cold air
Spacecraft — Atmosphere
produces drag, oxidation from free oxygen atoms (these atoms in water break away, combine with iron, make rust)
Primary causes of atmospheric motion
heat & earth's motion (heat in atmosphere responsible for all weather processes)
latent heat of condensation
Water vapor condenses, heat is released and effects temperature
Heat balance — what is it?

The equilibrium between incoming solar radiation and heat radiated back out. Without it the earth would grow steadily warmer. The processes maintaining it are also chiefly responsible for worldwide weather.
Centrifugal force

acts on air moving in curved path, decreases speed in low pressure, increases in high pressure (air flows clockwise around high pressure [anticyclone] and counterclockwise around low pressure [cyclone] in N Hemisphere)
The atmosphere and space as one medium — the term
AEROSPACE.
Precipitation vs condensation
If visible water FALLS it is precipitation; if it does NOT fall it is condensation.
What is the dew point spread?
The difference between the actual temperature and the dew point temperature.
Four ways atmospheric regions are classified

By TEMPERATURE (troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere); by PHYSICOCHEMICAL processes (ozonosphere, ionosphere, neutrosphere, chemosphere); by MOLECULAR COMPOSITION (homosphere, heterosphere); by DYNAMIC AND KINETIC processes (exosphere).
Four kinds of heat transfer — discriminate
CONDUCTION: heating by direct contact. ADVECTION: LATERAL (horizontal) transfer. CONVECTION: transfer by VERTICAL motion. RADIATION: heat energy of the sun reaching the earth.
Coriolis effect — the correct statement
The earth's rotation deflects anything moving over its surface. In the NORTHERN hemisphere, to the RIGHT of the direction of motion.
Centrifugal effect on curved airflow
DECREASES speed within a LOW-pressure area; INCREASES it within a HIGH-pressure area.
High vs low — the exact definitions
A HIGH is a center of high pressure surrounded by LOWER pressure. A LOW is a center of low pressure surrounded by HIGHER pressure. Reversing these is CAP's standard true/false trap.
Ridge, trough, col
RIDGE — elongated area of HIGH pressure. TROUGH — elongated area of LOW pressure. COL — the 'saddleback' area between a high and a low.
What is wind, in one word?
A HORIZONTAL movement of air. Friction tends to SLOW air movement.
Where is air density greatest, and why?
Near the earth's SURFACE — gravity pulls air downward.
What causes the land and sea-breeze phenomena?
Unequal heating by the sun of land and water areas.
Jet streams — the full picture

Narrow currents of high-speed air moving in a wavelike pattern, near 30,000 ft, generally west to east. They shift position frequently, MIGRATE WITH THE SEASONS, can be compared to a RIVER OF AIR, and affect the formation of cold and warm air masses — possibly acting as a barrier between cold air north and warm air south.
When does liquid water evaporate?
Only if there is SPACE in the air for the water vapor molecules to occupy. Air is saturated when it can hold no more.
Density — the plain-language definition
The comparison of how heavy something is to the space it fills.
Particulate matter — why it matters
Dust, dirt, smoke, exhaust or salt particles act as CONDENSATION NUCLEI. Without them, condensation and precipitation could not occur.
Temp — Stratosphere (and pause)
Classified by TEMPERATURE. Roughly 10-30 miles; temperature INCREASES through it. (Do not confuse with the ozonosphere, which occupies a similar altitude but is a PHYSICOCHEMICAL classification.)
Pressure
weight of molecules above press down on those below
Mass
amount of material
Heat
sum total of energy of all moving molecules w/in a substance
Temperature
a measure that expresses an average of the energy of molecular motion

Maritime tropical.
Match the air mass — cold and dry
Continental polar. (Polar/tropical = temperature; maritime/continental = moisture.)
Body of air with the same temperature and moisture content; boundary between two of them
AIR MASS; the boundary is a FRONT.
The five fog types — discriminate

RADIATION: at night the land cools the air above it below the dew point (by conduction). ADVECTION: moist air BLOWN over a COLD SURFACE. UPSLOPE: moist air carried UP A MOUNTAIN until cooled. EVAPORATION (steam): COLD air over WARM WATER. HIGH-INVERSION: actually a CLOUD — condensation near the top of cool air capped by warmer air.
The three general cloud types, and how the rest are classified
CUMULUS (piling up of rounded masses), STRATUS (layered), CIRRUS (high, thin). All others derive from these three and are classified according to ALTITUDE.
Cloud altitude bands
LOW: 300-6,500 ft. MIDDLE: 6,500-20,000 ft. HIGH: above 20,000 ft.
Which clouds are closest to the surface?
STRATUS and CUMULUS.
Which clouds have NO precipitation associated with them?
CIRRUS, CIRROSTRATUS and CIRROCUMULUS — the high, ice-crystal clouds.
Which cloud is most associated with violent weather?
CUMULONIMBUS. When it builds further it is called a thunderstorm.
Stratocumulus and altostratus — what precipitation?
STRATOCUMULUS: RAIN or SNOW, thick and bumpy, with turbulence — a warning. ALTOSTRATUS: moderate surface precipitation, thin, smooth.
Cold front vs warm front

COLD: oriented NORTHWEST to SOUTHEAST; denser air pushes UNDER the warm air abruptly → thunderstorms; cold masses move FASTER. WARM: tied to a LOW-pressure cell, extends eastward and travels northeast; less dense, slides OVER in a shallow wedge → low cloud, gentle rain, fog; temperature RISES afterward.
Stationary and occluded fronts

STATIONARY: the air masses have lost their punch and are no longer replacing one another — LITTLE movement along the edge; almost any light weather. OCCLUDED: a WARM air mass sandwiched between TWO COLD masses and lifted.
Lenticular — what shape, and where?
LENS-shaped (not concave). Forms where strong winds sweep up over high mountains. A ROTOR cloud rotates about an axis PARALLEL to the mountain's linear shape.
Fracto — meaning
BROKEN or RAGGED. It is NOT restricted to rain clouds.
Wind shear — in which directions?
Changes in wind speed and direction HORIZONTALLY, DOWNWARDLY and UPWARDLY — all of these.
Microburst — what is it associated with?
THUNDERSTORMS. A column of air rapidly cooled, descending toward the earth. A downdraft shear phenomenon.
Are turbulence classifications the same for all pilots?
NO — light, moderate and severe depend on the aircraft and the pilot. Terrain factors may cause clear air turbulence.
Wake turbulence — when is it produced?
By large aircraft IN FLIGHT generally, not only on landing. Air around the wingtips forms a vortex of tremendous energy.
Windward vs leeward — which is safer for a small aircraft?
WINDWARD. Rising windward air cools and loses moisture with LOW turbulence; descending leeward air warms, absorbs moisture, and has HIGH turbulence.
El Nino vs La Nina
EL NINO: warm waters move in and displace colder waters off South America for longer than normal. LA NINA: the opposite — colder than normal for longer than normal. Both affect weather worldwide.
Alto
high, but not highest
Front — Cold
NW-SE; energy of front depends on amount of cold air in high pressure cell behind; cold air denser, pushes under warm air; brings thunderstorms
Front — Stationary
fronts lose punch, not replacing each other; maybe slow thunderstorms, drizzle, fog, almost any form of weather
Fog — High-inversion
low cloud; condensation of vapor near top of cool air covered by warmer air
Fog — Upslope
moist air carried up slope, air is cooled
Air Mass characteristics depend
surface formed over, season, surface traveling over, length of time from source; (to E)

sections.name: Ch 21 — Rocket Fundamentals  —  3 of 60 exam questions
cards: Gravitation
describes force of attraction existing between all matter w/in universe
Gravity
when gravitation involves earth and a body or mass on or near earth, gravitation is called gravity
Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation
two bodies attract each other with a force directly proportional to their mass, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them [F=(GM1GM2)/d2]
Combustion Chamber
rocket fuel burns here, gases produced are very hot and create high pressure inside
Throat
as exhaust moves out, throat constricts exhaust to increase velocity
Nozzle
bell shaped nozzle allows exhaust to expand, lowering pressure (pressure inside is lower, only rearward motion)
Payload
whatever the rocket is carrying (satellites, astronauts, data, etc.); the four systems exist to deliver it
Impulse — what does it measure?

How much THRUST will be obtained from a propellant. SPECIFIC impulse (Isp) is the pounds of thrust from burning one pound of propellant for one second. DENSITY impulse measures thrust relative to the VOLUME the propellant occupies.
Specific Impulse

(Isp) number of pounds of thrust delivered by consuming one pound propellant (oxidizer/fuel) in one second; Isp following number means seconds during which 1lb thrust is provided by burning 1lb propellant; ie, 500Isp: burning 1lb produces 1lb thrust for 500sec (or 500lb for 1sec)
Density Impulse
another measure of propellant's thrust according to volume involved
Rocket
power plant used to propel payload, by principle of action and reaction
Missile
rocket propelled with warhead or weapon as payload (if payload is satellite, the vehicle is a launcher/booster)
Systems — Fuel
delivery of fuel to engine; tanks mix with air, draw into combustion chamber; can gravity feed, but many use pumps
Newton's law of Motion — 1

A body in the state of rest and a body in motion tend to remain at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by some outside force (inertia, or tendency of all things to remain in a fixed condition) [when launching, propulsion must produce enough force to overcome inertia]
Newton's law of Motion — 2

The rate of change in the momentum of a body is proportional to the force acting upon the body and is in the direction of the force. [FuMA, Force proportional to mass times acceleration; force required depends on mass]
Newton's law of Motion — 3
To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction [action of rocket engine produces forward motion] heart of rocketry
Airframe
contains other systems and provides streamlined shape
Propulsion
includes propellant, plumbing, engine; anything associated w/ propelling rocket
Propulsion — Chemical
mixing and burning chemical fuel and oxidizer to produce hot expanding gases
Propulsion — Gas-heating
external source to heat and cause propellant to build pressure necessary to provide thrust by exiting nozzle at high velocity
Propulsion — Electric
magnetic fields and currents to propel matter in small amounts
Guidance — Inertial
self-contained, senses rockets motion, fed to computer; impulses for correction are sent to control
Guidance — Command
guided to targets by command of human director (probably short range)
Guidance — Homing
Home in on target radiating light or heat
Guidance — Beam-rider
fly along a beam aimed at and kept on target
Konrad Kyeser von Eichstadt
devised gunpowder propelled rocket
William Hale
spin stabilization, angles exhaust tubes that spun during flight
Konstantin Eduardovich Tsiolkovsky
Russian scientist, first computations for rocket flights into space, solved theoretically how reaction engines could escape from and reenter earth's atmosphere
reaction engine
The action or a rocket's exhaust produces a reaction, the moving of the rocket in opposite direction
To increase thrust of rocket
increase mass of exhaust, or accelerate exhaust to higher velocity
Takeoff mass
payload, fuel load, dead weight
Who dropped weights from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, and what did it prove?
GALILEO — that objects of varying weights strike the ground at the same time if released together.
Match the rocketry pioneer — first rocket propelled by gunpowder
Konrad Kyeser von Eichstadt.
Match the rocketry pioneer — built the first viable launching pad
Colonel William Congreve. He also standardized gunpowder composition and added guide sticks, raising range from 300 yards to several thousand.
Match the rocketry pioneer — used spin stabilization
William Hale — by angling the exhaust tubes so the rocket spun.
Match the rocketry pioneer — first computations for rocket flight into space
Konstantin Tsiolkovsky.
Match the rocketry pioneer — developed a method to correct deviations from flightpath
Dr. Robert Goddard, the Father of Modern Rocketry, first to use liquid propellants.
Match the rocketry pioneer — used more powerful liquid propellants
Dr. Hermann Oberth — liquid oxygen and alcohol, 1920s, after Goddard.
Force, velocity, acceleration, momentum — the four definitions
FORCE: the cause of motion. VELOCITY: the rate a body moves when force is applied. ACCELERATION: the application of force over TIME. MOMENTUM: the PRODUCT of mass and velocity.
Which is NOT a major rocket system?
The PAYLOAD. The four are airframe, propulsion, guidance and control — they exist to deliver the payload.
Which is NOT a rocket propulsion system?
NUCLEAR. The three are chemical, gas-heating and electric.
Which is NOT part of the guidance system?
Controls for the engine. Guidance contains a computer, an inertial platform, and possibly a star-tracking unit.
The airframe must be...
Strong and LIGHTWEIGHT (not heavyweight). It provides a streamlined shape, contains the other systems, and withstands heat, stress and vibration.
Which system is the brain, and which executes?
GUIDANCE is the brain. CONTROL carries out what guidance dictates.
Which force did Newton identify as the tendency of a rotating body to move away from its center of rotation?
CENTRIFUGAL force.
Why was the rocket replaced as a significant military weapon?
Rockets of that era COULD NOT HIT A SPECIFIC TARGET — they were not accurate enough for precision bombardment. Artillery, which developed far greater ACCURACY, displaced them.
How are propellants classified?
As either SOLID or LIQUID.
Rockets first attached to aircraft in which war?
WORLD WAR I.
Atlas rocket — what was unusual about its skin?
So thin that if not loaded with propellants it had to be PRESSURIZED to keep from collapsing.
Four guidance types — discriminate

INERTIAL: self-contained, senses the rocket's own motion. COMMAND: guided by a human director, probably short range. HOMING: homes on a target radiating LIGHT or HEAT. BEAM-RIDER: flies ALONG A BEAM aimed at the target.
Two ways to increase thrust
Increase the MASS of exhaust expelled, or accelerate the exhaust to a HIGHER VELOCITY.
Force — definition
The CAUSE of motion. You experience it by exerting muscle to move yourself or an object.
Why were early rockets abandoned as military weapons?
They could not hit a specific target — not accurate enough for precision bombardment, even with improvements over stick (skyrocket-type) stabilization.
What did Tsiolkovsky do in 1903, and what did he never do?

Made the FIRST COMPUTATIONS for rocket flights into space and solved theoretically how reaction engines could escape from and reenter the earth's atmosphere. He NEVER BUILT a rocket, though he designed several.

sections.name: Ch 23 — Orbits and Trajectories  —  2 of 60 exam questions
cards: Orbit
path described by one body in its revolution about another body
Circular Orbit
orbit maintaining virtually constant altitude above earth's surface
Elliptical Orbit
any closed orbit that is not circular; will have an apogee and perigee
Equatorial Orbit
Satellite travels from West to East over earth's equator; some incline to equator a certain # degrees
Escape trajectory

The path taken when a vehicle MUST reach escape velocity (about 25,000 mph) to launch to the moon or another body. Velocity is so high, and inertia so great, that it comes under another body's gravity before reaching apogee.
Apogee
Point in orbital trajectory or flight path when body is most distant from body being orbited (for earth)
Perigee
Point in orbital trajectory or flight path when body is closest to body being orbited (for earth)
Velocity requirement
velocity required in order to travel a certain path
Escape velocity
requires for payload to escape from gravitational attraction of the planet
Burnout (velocity)
the moment rocket engine ceases to produce thrust, it's at burnout; velocity required to place craft on intended trajectory must be attained at burnout
Total velocity requirements
adding together the velocity requirements for all stages of the mission
Retrothrust
opposite direction thrust
Ballistics
the study of the arc of a nonorbiting body; primarily concerned with propelling an object from one place on earth's surface to another (no longer powered, under influence of natural forces)
Coplanar transfer
transfer (moving from one orbit to another) w/in same orbital plane
Geostationary Orbit
orbit stationed above one point on earth's surface equatorial orbit, revolution takes 24hrs. Valuable for communications, receivers/transmitters lock on and never loose contact; limited # positions
Geosynchronous vs geostationary orbit

GEOSYNCHRONOUS: orbital period matches the earth's 24-hour rotation. GEOSTATIONARY: a geosynchronous orbit ALSO over the EQUATOR, so the satellite appears to hover above one fixed point. Only a limited number of geostationary slots exist.
Polar orbit
crosses or nearly crosses M and S poles w/ each orbit; can photograph earth's entire surface
Sunsynchronous orbit
polar orbit, constantly exposed to sun (sunlight can generate for onboard operations; monitor sun activities, in space electrical power generation, etc.)
Remaining in Orbit
gravity pulls something to earth's surface at the same rate earth's surface curves. Thus objects remains at consistent altitude from surface, though falling towards surface
Two basic orbit types
elliptical and circular
Hohmann Transfer
place in low elliptical parking orbit, when at perigee, push vehicle to apogee of desired orbit; when reaches high point, thrust again and move out on circle tangent to transfer ellipse
Fast Transfer

trajectory chosen that intersects the two orbits; in direct ascent, more launch given than needed for apogee; at desired altitude, kick applied lower than apogee, with deflected thrust to aim to desired circle. Energy not in straight line, so extra energy needed; boosts to higher orbit faster than H transfer.
Non-coplanar transfer

Changes the ORBITAL PLANE. Launches from the Cape begin at a minimum inclination ANGLE of about 28.5 degrees. Thrust is applied at one of the two points where the vehicle crosses the EQUATOR — kicking it sideways, sometimes over several passes.
Which direction should rockets be fired, and how much does it add?
EAST, to take advantage of the earth's rotation. At the Equator this adds roughly 1,000 mph.
Increase orbital velocity — what happens?
The vehicle goes into a HIGHER orbit — which is also SLOWER.
Moving from a higher orbit to a lower orbit — the full chain
Requires RETROTHRUST, causing the vehicle to SLOW DOWN, making it more subject to GRAVITY — but as a result of the lower orbit the vehicle actually goes FASTER.
Why do higher orbits need lower velocity?
Because the gravitational effect WEAKENS with distance.
Match: path described by one body revolving about another
ORBIT. (A TRAJECTORY is the path of a body through the atmosphere or outer space.)
Match: satellite travels west to east around 0 degrees latitude
EQUATORIAL orbit.
Match: maintained at virtually constant altitude above the surface
CIRCULAR orbit. (ELLIPTICAL is any non-circular path around a body.)
Match: path a body takes, accelerating enough to overcome gravity's pull
ESCAPE TRAJECTORY. Escape velocity is about 25,000 mph.
Which orbit lets a satellite photograph the earth's entire surface?
POLAR.
Another name for the Hohmann transfer
MINIMUM ENERGY transfer. Thrust at perigee to raise apogee, then again at apogee to circularize.
Coplanar vs non-coplanar transfer
COPLANAR — within the SAME orbital plane. NON-COPLANAR — changes the plane; thrust applied as the vehicle crosses the EQUATOR. Launches from the Cape start at about 28.5 degrees inclination.
Fast transfer vs Hohmann
A fast transfer INTERSECTS both orbits rather than being tangent — it arrives sooner but requires MORE energy. It is substantially different from a Hohmann, not slightly.
Three components of takeoff mass
Payload, propellant load and deadweight.
Sounding rocket — purpose and trajectory
Sent on a SUBORBITAL trip to gather information; trajectory is typically STRAIGHT UP.
Ballistic flight — definition and everyday example
Propelling an object from the earth's surface to NON-ORBITAL space flight. A bullet fired horizontally from a rifle is a good example.
Inertia
tendency of body at rest to remain at rest, body in motion to remain in motion in straight line, constant velocity
Who are the current and emerging launch services providers?
UNITED LAUNCH ALLIANCE (a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed-Martin), BLUE ORIGIN, and SPACEX. NASA hires them rather than building and operating its own launch fleet.
Which launch vehicles does NASA currently use for its payloads?
ANTARES, PEGASUS, TAURUS, ATHENA, ATLAS V, DELTA IV and FALCON 9.
The Falcon family — who builds it and what are the members?
SPACE EXPLORATION TECHNOLOGIES (SpaceX). Flown: FALCON I (no longer in production), FALCON 9, and FALCON HEAVY. In development: FALCON SUPER HEAVY and STARSHIP, being designed to be FULLY REUSABLE.
Vulcan — who is building it, and what are its figures?
UNITED LAUNCH ALLIANCE, based on the ATLAS design. Planned capability of 76,900 LBS to low Earth orbit, with first flight planned for 2021. ULA currently offers the Delta IV and Atlas V.
New Glenn — who is building it, and why does it matter?

BLUE ORIGIN, from a new rocket factory next to Kennedy Space Center, launching from an upgraded LAUNCH COMPLEX 36 at Cape Canaveral. Once operational it will be the LARGEST, MOST POWERFUL rocket ever launched from Cape Canaveral — 99,000 LBS to low Earth orbit.
Which Blue Origin rocket is in advanced development besides New Glenn?
NEW SHEPARD.

sections.name: Ch 24 — Space Environment  —  4 of 60 exam questions
cards: Cislunar space
space between earth and moon (magnetosphere, protons and electrons, magnetic lines, radiation storms, cosmic rays, sun's photons)
Interstellar space
distance between extent of one solar system and beginning of another
Thermonuclear reaction
nuclear fusion of atoms under pressure and heat into different atoms
Solar winds

charged particles ejected from sun flowing continuously through interplanetary space; extension of cornea into interplanetary space; bow shock wave where magnetic lines of force of magnetic field are struck by solar plasma
Ion

atom carrying positive or negative charge as result of losing or gaining one or more electrons (caused by powerful ultraviolet radiation of sun, ultra high frequency of cosmic rays from stars of outer space
Magnetosphere
region of earth's atmosphere where ionized gas plays a big part in the dynamics of the atmosphere and where the geomagnetic field plays an important role
Cosmic Rays
energetic charged particles from all over galaxy and beyond rain down on earth atomic particles, mostly electrons and nuclei
Polar Magnetic Storms

solar disturbances observable only in polar areas; produce sporadic radiation emissions from upper atmosphere over middle and high latitudes; cause Aurora Borealis (N) and Australis (S) (interaction of solar radiation and earth's magneticism)
Scintillation
electron density variations in the ionosphere cause rapid changes in radio signals
Outgassing
removing pressure, bubbles of gas escape
Cold welding
moving parts fit with tiny amount of air between; air escapes and they weld together (need lubricant)
Free fall
subject to gravity, but we and our craft are falling together w/ nothing to resist
Intergalactic space
space between galaxies
Reasons to exploit space
global view of earth; see universe more clearly; abundant resources; making new materials
Sun — size and gravity
A medium-sized star, diameter about 864,000 miles — more than 100 times earth's. Strongest gravitational force in the solar system; its gravity controls the orbital paths of all objects in it.
Sun — magnetic activity and cycles
Magnetic field more than 100 times stronger than earth's, lacking definite structure. Its rotation alters the magnetic fields. Rotation averages about 27 days; sunspot cycle about 11 years.
Sun's atmosphere — Photosphere
thin shell which gives light
Sun's atmosphere — Chromosphere
sphere of color, spicules
Sun's atmosphere — Corona
enormous area of faint white light visibly extending outward from surface
Sun Phenomena — Sunspots
on photosphere; dark spots, cooler than surrounding plasma
Sun Phenomena — Prominences
Hot spots shown as bright blotches, ionized gases flowing down magnetic lines: against black background
Sun Phenomena — Filaments
against solar disk (appear darker)
Sun Phenomena — Solar Flares
Bursting from surface, extend through chromosphere into corona
Ionospheric behavior

Sunspots, solar flares, and other disturbances produce fluctuations in output of sun's rays; these produce Sudden Ionospheric Disturbances (SIDs) and other variations; ionosphere blends with exosphere
Van Allen belts — shape and composition
Crescent-shaped in cross section, composed of TWO shells, with horns dipping toward the magnetic poles. Made of protons and electrons trapped by the earth's magnetic field.
Van Allen belts — how are they formed?

The sun emits charged particles (mainly protons and electrons) as plasma. More powerful cosmic rays enter the upper layers, collide with atmospheric molecules and release neutrons, which travel outward and decay into protons and electrons — then get trapped by the magnetic field.
Van Allen belts — the threat to astronauts
RADIATION, which may be as high as 65 TIMES the safe exposure. Safe is about 0.3 roentgens/hour; the inner belt runs 10-20 roentgens/hour. Also damages satellites.
Spacecraft — Vacuum
empty; causes outgassing, cold welding
Electric charging — Absolute
whole craft is charged (like when craft passes through fields of plasma such as solar wind; imparts negative charge on whole satellite)
Electric charging — Differential
one part gets charged and has different charge than rest of craft (usually negative on shaded sides due to plasma charging on sunlit sides)
Free fall (effects)
can cause dehydration (fluid distributes to upper body, eliminated), heart can weaken, dizziness
Radiation effects
safe is .3 roentgens per hour; internal belt gives 10-20 roentgens per hour; can damage satellites
Match the solar layer — enormous area of white light emanating from the sun's surface
CORONA. (The PHOTOSPHERE is the thin shell that gives light; the CHROMOSPHERE is characterized by SPICULES.)
Match — cooler area appearing dark on the photosphere
SUNSPOT.
Match — hair-like phenomena characterizing the chromosphere
SPICULES.
Match — non-cyclic eruptions that can harm space assets
SOLAR FLARES.
Match — steady emissions made up of many types of atoms and ions
SOLAR WINDS.
Match — areas of lower density in the sun's crown
CORONA HOLES.
Does the solar atmosphere include the core?
NO. The solar atmosphere is the PHOTOSPHERE, CHROMOSPHERE and CORONA. Including the core is CAP's trap.
Is the sun's output consistent?
No — it VARIES, and the variance DOES impact space operations.
How many other solar systems in our galaxy?
About 100 BILLION.
A parsec is how many light years? And a light year is how far?
A parsec is about THREE (3.26) light years. A light year is 5.878 TRILLION miles — the distance a photon travels in 365 earth days.
How far to the nearest solar system in our galaxy?
Just over FOUR light years.
Sun's diameter and magnetic field — compared with earth
Both more than ONE HUNDRED times earth's. Diameter about 864,000 miles.
Sun's rotation rate
Varies from about 25 days at the equator to about 35 at the poles; generally accepted average about 27 DAYS.
Sunspot cycle length
Varies, but usually close to an 11-YEAR cycle.
How fast does solar flare radiation reach earth?
The less dangerous ELECTROMAGNETIC radiation in as little as 8 MINUTES. The more dangerous high-energy PARTICLES take considerably longer.
Where does USAF say space begins, and why? Where do others say?
USAF: 50 MILES — because that is where it awards ASTRONAUT WINGS. Others: 62 miles / 100 km.
Magnetosphere — where does it begin and extend?
Begins about 217 miles above the surface, extending 10-15 earth radii to the boundary with interplanetary plasma. Struck by the SOLAR WIND it forms a BOW SHOCK WAVE, pushed out past the earth.
Van Allen belts — shape, structure, and threat

CRESCENT-shaped in cross section, composed of TWO shells, horns dipping to the magnetic poles. Protons and electrons. Their significant threat to astronauts is RADIATION — as high as 65 TIMES safe exposure.
Cosmic rays — speed, and what reduces them
Travel at nearly the speed of light; flow greatly reduced by the SOLAR WIND and the earth's MAGNETIC FIELD.
Magnetic storms — how fast do they develop?
Sudden onset of radiation bursts; the magnetic field undergoes marked change in AN HOUR OR LESS.
Which radio band is used for international broadcasting, and why?
SHORT-WAVE — it bounces off the ionosphere better. LONG-wave is used for LOCAL broadcasting. Reversing these is CAP's trap.
Outgassing vs cold welding

OUTGASSING: tiny bubbles of gas escape from spacecraft materials due to the VACUUM of space. COLD WELDING: the tiny amount of air between two surfaces escapes and they FUSE — prevented with a lubricant such as DRY GRAPHITE.
Absolute vs differential charging
ABSOLUTE: the WHOLE craft takes one uniform charge. DIFFERENTIAL: ONE PART has a different charge from another, often shaded vs sunlit surfaces.
Atom
most mass in central body, or nucleus, cluster of neutrons and protons; negatively charged electrons whirl around
Magnetosphere characteristics

like the effect of filaments producing cloud around magnet; N and S magnetic poles near the N and S celestial poles, rotational axis; tail pointing away from sun because of solar radiation pressure pushing out
What four things in the space environment take a toll on spacecraft?
The ATMOSPHERE, the VACUUM of space, CHARGED PARTICLES, and SPACE DEBRIS.
What two effects does the atmosphere have on a spacecraft?
DRAG, which slows the spacecraft — the same force felt on a hand held out of a moving car. And OXIDATION from free oxygen atoms, the same process that rusts iron.

sections.name: Ch 25 — Our Solar System and Beyond  —  4 of 60 exam questions
cards: Space
place that extends indefinitely in all directions and contains all of the stars, planets, and galaxies in universe (widly accepted: 62mi, or 100kl; wings to those who reach 50mi)
Interplanetary space
center of sun to orbit of outermost planet (solar system)
Milky Way
galaxy in which we live, along w/ 100billion other solar systems and stars; spiraling arms, center older, arms newer stars; halo of gas surrounds
Rille
long, irregular depressions similar to streambeds on earth
Planet
orbits sun; large enough for gravity to make round; cleared neighborhood of smaller objects
Asteroids
rocky and metallic bodies orbiting sun, too small to be planets; main belt BETWEEN Mars and Jupiter
Comet

small, irregularly shaped body whose nucleus is composed of water, ice, rock, and frozen gases (elliptical orbit, close to sun, often further than Pluto; develop coma when approaching sun; nucleus and coma form head; tail; Oort cloud produces long, possibly medium pulled to shorter orbits, range comets)
Micrometeoroids vs meteoroids vs meteors
MICROMETEOROIDS: the very small, dust-particle-size bits of matter. METEOROID: the name applied to clumps of matter in space from that size upward. A METEOR is one entering the atmosphere.
Nova
stars that aren't stable; flare, subside, flare
Supernova
gives up great mass, giant explosion of light/energy
Black Hole
probably large star that exhausted nuclear fuel and collapsed inward on self; force builds up enough to keep explosion from occurring, but nothing is allowed to leave from resulting gravity
Galaxy
grouping of billions of stars apparently merging into luminous band extending across sky
Air Characteristics — Pressure
higher altitude, less pressure
Air Characteristics — Temp
hotter air more energy; decreases 3.5F 1,000ft
Air Characteristics — Density
how much squeezed in volume heated, decrease in density (they move apart)
Air Characteristics — Viscosity
fluid's resistance to flow
Galileo (probe)
Launched to take direct measurements of Jupiter's atmosphere and explore its moons. Entered Jupiter orbit 1995.
Comet 1
first pure jet airliner
Titan IV

(all Titans started as twostage Titan II ICBM) stretched 1st and 2nd stage, 2 seven-segment solid strp on boosters, Centaur G third stage; can place 10,200lbs geosynchronous orbit, or 31,100 near earth orbit; Titans are largest, most powerful launch vehicles in US, only larger one was Saturn V Moon rocket
Vomit Comet
NASA's plane that flies high as can, then dives straight down to put passengers in 1min free fall
Voyager spacecraft
launched to study outer planets
Lafayette Escadrille
American volunteers flying for FRANCE in WORLD WAR I. Not France's own aces — Americans. Raoul Lufberry was a member.
Venus
nearest to earth in distance and size, sister; highly reflective atmosphere, strong greenhouse effect; mapped by Magellan probe
Mariner 2
confirmed high surface temp, first successful interplanetary mission
Venera 3
Soviet; crash landed
Mariner 5
carbon dioxide rich atmosphere
Mariner 10
direction/speed of clouds
Veneras 9 & 10
craters
Pioneer 1 (Venus)
tall mountains, plateaus, canyons
Pioneer 2 (Venus)
4 distinct could and haze layers
Magellan
mapped 99%
Galileo (Venus)
orbiter and space probe
Venus Express
ESA
Moon

same side towards earth, 270o during 14 earth days, equaling one moon day, -250o lunar night; impact craters; rillies; dust may have come from meteorites striking surface, or is picked up from space; tests showed dust to have sterilizing effect
Moon rocks
Basalt (dark gray, tiny holes gas escaped from; Anorthosite (commonest, feldspar, highlands and light areas); others include Breccia (combination) and KREEP (not on earth)
Mars
fourth planet, red planet; thin carbon dioxide atmosphere, half gravity of earth
Mariner (Mars)
4, flyby w/ 21 photos 6/7, 200 photos, clues for puzzling features 9, pics of entire surface
Pathfinder
rover Sojourner investigated rocks and soil
Global surveyor
entered orbit
Spirit and Opportunity
rovers landed 2004, exploring
Jupiter

largest planet: rotates 10hrs, bulges at equator; high winds, giant storms; hydrogen gass giant, w/ helium, methane, and ammonia; giant red spot; 16 known moons, larger four Galilean moons, rotate clockwise); Jupiter has strong magnetic field and radiation belts; like ALL gas giants, has RINGS
Voyager (Jupiter)
volcanic eruptions on Io, discovered three mons (to make 16)
Saturn — rings
Rings contain mostly ROCK AND ICE. Hundreds of narrow ringlets, about 1 mile thick, extending 250,000 miles from the planet. SEVEN distinct rings; the final two were discovered by Pioneer.
Saturn — the planet itself
Second largest. Rotates fast, about 10 hours; takes about 29 years to orbit the sun. LESS DENSE THAN WATER — it would float. About 18 moons; Titan has its own atmosphere.
Neptune — characteristics

The OUTERMOST gas planet and the FOURTH LARGEST in the solar system. Discovered in 1846 when scientists determined something was affecting the ORBIT OF URANUS. About 3 BILLION miles from the sun; takes 165 EARTH YEARS to orbit. So similar to Uranus the two are sometimes called TWINS.
Pluto

yellowish gold, Mars size; rotates 6.5 days, orbit inclined to elliptic 17o, bringing it inside Neptune sometimes during 249yr orbit; 50-75% rock mixed with ice; temp varies widely; atmosphere freezes as moves away from sun; minor planets lie beyond Pluto, Kuiper Belt. New Horizons launched towards Pluto
Eris
dwarf has moon
Sedna
most distant body recorded
Quaoar
edge of Kuiper belt, in field of icy bodies
Water on Mars — the precise claim
Water HAS been found, but NOT in liquid form. The Vikings found more water than expected.
What gives Mars its red color, and what were the reddish areas once thought to be?
IRON gives the red color. The reddish areas were once thought to be DESERTS. Highest surface content: silicon and iron.
Mariner 4 — first what?
First CLOSE-UP PHOTOGRAPHS of another planet.
Match the lunar rock — found mainly on the moon's plains
BASALT — dark gray, tiny holes where gas escaped.
Match the lunar rock — composed mostly of feldspar, makes up the highlands
ANORTHOSITE — the most common lunar rock.
Match the lunar rock — abundant on the moon, cannot be found on Earth
KREEP. (BRECCIA is a combination of fragments.)
Three new minerals discovered in lunar samples
Pyroxferroite, armalcolite and tranquillityite.
Are lunar rocks older or younger than Earth rocks?
OLDER.
Moon — gravity, faces, day/night range
Gravity is ONE-SIXTH of Earth's. We see only ONE side, always the SAME side. Day/night difference roughly 500 degrees F (about 270 down to -250).
Rilles
Long, irregular DEPRESSIONS on the moon, similar to streambeds.
What does 'asteroid' mean, and which was found first?
It means STARLIKE. CERES was the first discovered. The main belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
Comets — orbit shape, tail, how long observed
Orbits are ECCENTRIC. The tail forms as the comet nears THE SUN. Observed SINCE ANCIENT TIMES. Long-period comets come from the Oort cloud.
Jupiter — the four numbers
Rotates in about 10 HOURS (very rapidly, bulging at the equator). Makes up about 70 PERCENT of the mass of all the planets. Has the MOST INTENSE radiation belts of any planet. 16 known moons.
Saturn — rings, density, period
Rings contain mostly ROCK AND ICE. LESS DENSE THAN WATER — it would float. About 29 years to orbit; rotates in about 10 hours.
Uranus — rings and moons before and after Voyager

Before Voyager: 9 rings and 5 moons known. VOYAGER 2 revealed 2 MORE RINGS and 10 MORE MOONS. Later observation has brought the total known moons to 27. Voyager 2 also found its magnetic field tilted 60 degrees and offset from center.
Neptune and Uranus — why are they called twins?
They are so similar in size and composition that they are sometimes called TWINS. Neptune is the outermost gas planet and fourth largest; discovered 1846 from its effect on Uranus's orbit.
Discriminate: nova, supernova, pulsar, quasar, black hole, nebula

NOVA — a binary star cycling in varying brightness. SUPERNOVA — an exploding star. PULSAR — flashes electromagnetic emissions in set patterns. QUASAR — extremely luminous body. BLACK HOLE — the ultimate star, which cannot radiate anything. NEBULAE — clouds of matter not yet formed into stars.
Intragalactic vs interstellar space
INTRAGALACTIC — the space WITHIN galaxies. INTERSTELLAR — between the extent of one solar system and another.
The 2004 Mars rovers
SPIRIT and OPPORTUNITY. (Not 'Faith'.) Sojourner was the earlier Pathfinder rover.
Pluto and the Kuiper Belt

Pluto reclassified by some scientists as a DWARF PLANET. The Kuiper Belt extends BILLIONS of miles beyond Neptune's orbit; Quaoar sits at its edge; Sedna is the most distant body recorded; Eris is a dwarf with a moon.
Vikings 1 and 2 — what did each consist of?
ORBITERS and LANDERS. The orbiters surveyed the planet and relayed data gathered by the landers.
Earth — the basic figures
About 70% water, of which the Pacific is roughly half. Rotates in 24 hours, spinning EASTWARD; revolves around the sun in about 365 days.
How many moons did Jupiter have before the Voyager flights?
13 known satellites. Four are large and bright enough to be seen from earth — the Galilean moons.
Voyager — launch date and mission
The first of two Voyager spacecraft launched 4 JANUARY 1979 on a long mission to study the OUTER PLANETS — Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus, and their moons.
Jupiter's magnetic field — what is unusual about it?
It is OPPOSITE that of Earth — the north magnetic pole is at the SOUTH pole of Jupiter.

sections.name: Ch 26 — Unmanned Exploration  —  4 of 60 exam questions
cards: Density
indicates how tightly the particles of mater are packed together (decreases w/ altitude)
ISS Agreement

1988, US provides management for building of International Space Station, along with Japan ESA, Canada, Russia (1993); new agreement 1998; detailed who bears what cost, managing station through consensus, jurisdiction over own station elements, compromise for military involvement (owner decides peaceful/not)
Satellite
natural or artificial object that orbits earth
Atlantic crossing
Curtiss flying boats NY-England; Reed made it; 2weeks later, nonstop cross, John Alcock, Arthur Brown
Longitudinal axis / Aileron
Roll
Attitude indicator
artificial horizon basic, most important
Cumulonimbus
cumulus built up; precipitation, thunder, lightning; w/ further building/increase, called a thunderstorm
Soviet Union's efforts

upper atmosphere research with captured V-2s; improved V-2 called T-1, in 1954 worked on multistage; 1956, had ICBM, soon to come nuclear warheads; October 4, 1957 Sputnik (we reacted immediately; to launch vanguard 1 from Cape Canaveral; exploded, launched Explorer 1 Jan 31, 1958)
Three principles of space law
freedom of use (all nations have access); non-appropriation (no one owns space); common interests (all nations should share in benefits)
1967 Outer Space Treaty

principle of freedom of use, space is "providence of all mankind"; exploration should benefit all; all three principles in written form, legitimizes military presence in space (addressed accidents/emergencies)
1972 ABM Treaty

US and USSR agreed not to develop or test Anti-Ballistic Missile systems. It SANCTIONED the use of satellites to monitor other countries for treaty compliance — national technical means were PERMITTED, not banned.
NASA Act
Commercial Space Launch Act
promote private sector activity; US citizen or org. must be licensed to conduct space ops. CSLA authorized military to provide support/facilities for commercial launches
Four satellite categories
Communication, observation, navigation, scientific
INTELSAT
Satellites, and organization; International Telecommunications Satellite Organization, links telecommunication networks via global satellite system of geostationary satellites
TDRSS

(Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System) three satellites and ground station; simultaneous, full time coverage for Space Shuttle and up to 25 other low orbiting spacecraft (Galaxy distributed cable TV) assists DSN
DSN (Deep Space Network)
supported deep space probes 1959, supported all Apollo missions
Navigation (TRANSIT and TIMATION)
TRANSIT [update internal navigation system on Polaris] and TIMATION [two-dimensional, got lat/long] early designs
NAVSTAR GPS — origin and description (Ch 26)

A space-based radio-positioning system. Directed 1974, first Navstar launched 1978. Managed by the Navstar GPS Joint Program Office, Los Angeles AFB. Provides navigation and timing to civilian AND military users worldwide. Satellites orbit every 12 HOURS. Ch 26 states a constellation of 24 satellites.
Observation (categories)
Weather, Multi-spectrum imaging, reconnaissance
Weather satellites — what do they measure?
Temperature at the surface and in the atmosphere, cloud cover, moisture levels, and lightning.
Weather satellites — name the programs

TIROS was the first; NIMBUS measured radiation. NOAA operates advanced TIROS-N craft with search-and-rescue capability. GOES is the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite. The military equivalent is DMSP.
Multi-spectrum imaging satellites
Observe radiant energy to give information on crops, ocean currents and natural resources. LANDSAT satellites locate natural resources and monitor conditions on the earth's surface.
Scientific (satellites)
gain information; orbital astronomy or environmental analysis
Explorers

1 discovered van Allen belts, 3 orbited in 1958 and gave more info on radiation, 6 first photographs of earth from space; they were essential to understanding space environment before astronauts were sent out
Orbiting Solar Observatory (OSO)
sun studied
Orbiting Astronomical Observatory (OAO)
broadened understanding of universe; stars in ultraviolet, infrared, gamma, x-ray wavelengths; extend knowledge of gasses, confirmed predicted hydrogen clouds around comets
High-energy Astronomy Observatory (HEAO)
investigate sources and intensities of high energy radiation at far end of electromagnetic spectrum
Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer
explorer class, continuation of strides made in x-ray astronomy thru using satellites
Hubble Space Telescope
built to work like ground observatory, free from atmospheric interference, 310mi employed by Discovery
Solar Mesosphere explorer
studies reactions of sunlight and atmosphere
Earth Observing System (EOS)

study earth as complete environmental system; was called Earth Science Enterprise; has observation satellites, data system, scientists; data collected from existing satellites and space shuttle, specialized satellites also gather data; fist system to give integrated measurements of earth's systems
Rangers
early probes, investigated moon
Surveyors
concentrated attention to moon, landed on surface, soft landers; had to know what module would encounter
Lunar Orbiters
photos of moon's surface so maps were made (flyby; above landed ?)
Mariners
inner planets, 10 flew by Venus/Mercury
Pioneers
outer and inner; 10, first close up photos of Jupiter; 11, trajectory to Saturn
Vikings
1&2 explored Mars, searched for life
Voyagers 1&2
greatly improved pics and data on Pioneers opening to outer planets; 2 flew by Uranus
Giotto
explored Halley's Comet
Mars Global Surveyor
mapped and collected info on surface of Mars; also atmosphere, gravity, magnetic fields, etc.
Mars Pathfinder
second of low-cost Discovery missions; stationary lander and surface rover
Cassini
Saturn; international between NASA, ESA, and other European partners
Chandra
new x-ray observatory
X-Prize
10million to first non-government reusable manned craft launched to 62km, and return w/in 2weeks, w/ weight of 3 adult humans November 6, 2004 was awarded to Mojave Aerospace Ventures, SpaceShipOne
Thor-Delta — what is it and what can it lift?

Thor with second and third stages became Thor-Delta. The first Delta could put a 480 lb payload into a 300-mile orbit. Delta II is a three-stage booster with nine solid strap-ons, able to place 2,000 lbs into a 22,000-mile orbit.
Atlas — what firsts is it associated with?
Launched the world's first communications satellite (1958). Boosted Project Mercury. Also launched the first spacecraft to Venus, Mercury, Mars and Jupiter.
Sputnik
first artificial satellite, October 4th, 1957
Explorer 1
our first satellite, January 31, 1958
Zero
Japanese reconnaissance? Precision (precise); area (against Japan)?
SOHO
Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, Dec 1995
Spitzer space telescope
launched to orbit 2003
Sputnik (custom)
established important new custom of satellites to fly over countries w/o permission (freedom of use)
Vikings 1/2
orbiters and landers both; orbiters surveyed planet, relayed pics/data gathered by landers below; more water than expected; Viking 1 found -18 thru -130 degrees
Pioneers 10/11 (Jupiter)
first investigated; discovered that banded structure lack near poles, for circular/oval patterns
Probe vs satellite
PROBES travel BEYOND earth's orbit. SATELLITES orbit the earth.
Match the probe — first close-up pictures of the moon
RANGERS (they crashed deliberately while transmitting).
Match the probe — information helped Apollo planners know what to expect
SURVEYORS — soft landers.
Match the probe — five probes, 1966-67, photographed the moon's entire surface
LUNAR ORBITERS.
Match the probe — flyby missions to Mercury and Venus
MARINERS. Mariner 2 was the first successful interplanetary mission.
Match the probe — first close-up pictures of Jupiter and Saturn
PIONEERS.
Match the probe — flew past Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus, now headed for interstellar space
VOYAGERS. Voyager also found volcanic eruptions on Io.
Match the probe — ESA mission to Halley's Comet
GIOTTO.
Match the probe — 1996, Martian geology, resources, climate and weather
MARS GLOBAL SURVEYOR.
Match the probe — first rover on another planet for rock and soil experiments
PATHFINDER (rover: Sojourner).
Match the probe — direct measurements of Jupiter's atmosphere and its moons
GALILEO.
Match the probe — international robotic probe to Saturn's rings, atmosphere, magnetosphere
CASSINI.
Match the probe — orbiters and landers at Mars, tested soil samples
VIKINGS.
Match the observatory — discovered the Van Allen belts
EXPLORER I. (Explorer 6 returned the first photographs of earth from space.)
Match the observatory — discovered a gamma ray burst from Galaxy Centaurus A
HIGH ENERGY ASTRONOMY OBSERVATORY.
Match the observatory — solved light pollution and atmospheric interference
HUBBLE SPACE TELESCOPE, operating about 300 miles up.
Match the observatory — improved knowledge of interstellar gases
ORBITING ASTRONOMICAL OBSERVATORY.
Match the observatory — studied the sun's protection of x-rays and gamma rays
ORBITING SOLAR OBSERVATORY.
Match the observatory — sunlight and the earth's ozone layer
SOLAR MESOSPHERE EXPLORER.
Match the observatory — interaction of earth and radiation energy from the sun
EARTH RADIATION BUDGET SATELLITE.
Match the observatory — how air, land, water and life interact on earth
EARTH OBSERVING SYSTEM.
Match the observatory — from LEO, studies white dwarfs, black holes, active galactic nuclei
X-RAY TIMING EXPLORER (Rossi).
Sort the satellites by type
WEATHER: DMSP, GOES, Nimbus, TIROS. MULTI-SPECTRUM IMAGING: Landsat, SPOT. RECONNAISSANCE: DSP.
DMSP — what is it and who gets the data?
Defense Meteorological Satellite Program — WEATHER data exclusively to the Department of Defense.
First telecommunications satellite
TELSTAR 1.
Active vs passive communications satellites
PASSIVE reflect the signal. ACTIVE AMPLIFY it before return.
Which is NOT a source of space law?
UN DECREES. The sources are TREATIES, CUSTOMS, INTERNATIONAL COURTS and opinio juris.
Which ITU policy conflicted with which principle of space law?
'First come, first served' in assigning GEOSTATIONARY ORBITS conflicted with the NON-APPROPRIATION principle. Eight equatorial nations responded with the Bogata Declaration of 1976.
Two purposes of scientific satellites
ORBITAL ASTRONOMY and ENVIRONMENTAL ANALYSIS. They gather information that may or may not have immediate use.
What are L4 and L5, and what are they for?
Points of gravitational EQUILIBRIUM, named for Lagrange — the most likely potential place for SPACE COLONIES.
Which launch agency has only recently been acknowledged to exist?
NATIONAL SECURITY.
Which ISS partner began participating in 1993?
RUSSIA. The original 1988 agreement was US, Japan, ESA and Canada; a new agreement followed in 1998.
Land Remote Sensing Commercialization Act — what did it do?
ALL of: allowed the sale of government data; set limits on the quality of data sold; directed that data be provided to all customers at the SAME cost.
What did Sputnik establish in international law?
The right of satellites to OVERFLY other nations without permission — the practical origin of the freedom-of-use principle.
Reconnaissance satellites — beyond photos and infrared
Detect NUCLEAR EXPLOSIONS, conduct ELECTRONIC reconnaissance, and provide EARLY WARNING of missile launches.
NASA
launches nonmilitary spacecraft
National Aeronautics and Space Act Law
Eisenhower, July 29, 1958; legal basis for military and civil space activities
Probe
spacecraft that either fly by, orbit, or land on celestial body other than earth
America's early space efforts

Army assembles scientists/engineers White Sands Proving grounds NM 1946 to research upper atmosphere; Navy researched to build improved V-2, called Viking; Army developed Redstone Missile, 1953, 200mi, 3000mph; Air Force researched Intercontinental Ballistic missiles (canceled); restarted, made Atlas, nucear warheads that could be mounted
GPS accuracy — what does the source say?

Accuracy varies with the USER'S EQUIPMENT and ATMOSPHERIC CONDITIONS. Civilian accuracy reported at better than 3 METERS horizontally. The US military has access to MULTI-CHANNEL GPS, which improves accuracy further.
What preceded Navstar, and who was directed to build it?

System 621B identified longitude, latitude and altitude — a three-dimensional, continuously running design. In 1974 the AIR FORCE was directed to create a new global navigation system combining the best features of earlier programs, assisted by the Defense Mapping Agency.

cards: International Telecommunications Union (ITU)
UN org. regulating international communications (radio, GEOs)
EVA
Extra-vehicular activity; EVA suits have own life support systems
MMU
Manned Maneuvering Unit, nitrogen propelled, hand-controlled device, allows more mobility than tethers
Effects on Communication
not all frequencies usable for uplink/downlink ground to satellite comm; scintillation; solar flares realease large amount of energy, hurts radio comm. Termed, Solar Radio Burst
Communication (SATCOM)
media transmission like radio, TV; data transmission like internet; cell phones; links to craft; Active if it amplifies signals; Passive if it just reflects
Defense Satellite Communication System (DSCS)
continuous long distance message service; exclusive comm to high gov.
Mercury (program)
to find out if humans could survive in space, effects of travel on the body
Gemini
improve for lunar mission, 2 people in space, rendezvous, and cock, first walk (1st 2man capsule, first walk)
Vostok
first soviet craft to take people to space
Voskhod
Soviet, 1964. Three-man capsule. First walk in space was made from it (Aleksei Leonov).
Salyut
space station (first ever) 1971. Soyuz with world's first space laboratory (being this)
Skylab (American station)
2yrs after Salyut, American space station
Launch vehicles
can be expendable (Titan, Atlas, Delta) or reusable (space shuttle)
Space suits — Mercury and Gemini

1930s high-altitude flyers wore pressure suits first. MERCURY astronauts wore a modified version of a NAVY high-altitude pressure suit. GEMINI suits were lighter, easily removable, and could be taken off in orbit.
Space Station Alpha
venture between US, Europe, Japan, Russia; permanent space station of near future
L4, L5
potential points for space colonies, gravitational equilibrium, named for Lagrange
Project Mercury
First US manned space program. Objective: find out whether humans could survive and function in space. Alan Shepard first American in space; John Glenn first American to orbit.
The three early US programs — one line each
MERCURY: first US manned flight; could humans survive in space? GEMINI: first to place TWO persons in space; rendezvous, docking, first American spacewalk. APOLLO: landed a man on the moon.
Match — first space station intended for prolonged occupancy
SALYUT. (MIR is the SECOND-generation Russian station.)
Match — transports up to three cosmonauts to and from space
SOYUZ (meaning 'union'), designed for docking.
Vostok vs Voskhod

VOSTOK — first Soviet craft to carry people into space; Vostok 6 carried Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman, 48 orbits over 3 days. VOSKHOD — first launched October 1964 with a THREE-MAN crew; from Voskhod 2 on 18 March 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, 12 MINUTES outside.
The four 'firsts' in space — Soviet and American
First man in space: GAGARIN. First American in space: SHEPARD. First American to orbit: GLENN. First Russian to walk in space: LEONOV. First American to walk in space: EDWARD WHITE.
The women's firsts in space (as given in the source)
First woman in space: VALENTINA TERESHKOVA, aboard Vostok 6 — 48 orbits over 3 days. First AMERICAN woman in space: DR. SALLY RIDE, aboard Challenger on STS-7.
Apollo 11 — date and order
20 July 1969. Neil Armstrong walked first, then Edwin Aldrin.
Apollo-Soyuz — what and when?
A linkup in space between an American and a Russian manned spacecraft, July 1975.
The Space Shuttle — formal name and three main components
SPACE TRANSPORTATION SYSTEM. Orbiter, EXTERNAL TANK, and SOLID ROCKET BOOSTERS.
Which was the first Space Shuttle, and what was it used for?
ENTERPRISE — atmospheric flight tests ONLY. The five operational orbiters: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis, Endeavour. Columbia flew STS-1, 1981.
Long-Duration Exposure Facility (LDEF)
Placed into space by the 11TH SPACE SHUTTLE MISSION to conduct experiments. It gathered long-term data on the space environment and its effects on space systems; it was retrieved a few years later.
Who built Spacelab?
The EUROPEAN SPACE AGENCY — an orbiting laboratory carried in the Shuttle bay.
What is the air inside space stations?
A mixture of OXYGEN and NITROGEN. Astronauts did NOT have to keep suits on at all times inside the Shuttle.
Skylab — purpose and construction
To place a LABORATORY in space. Built largely from LEFTOVER APOLLO parts. Followed Salyut by about two years.
X-Prize — winner, craft, terms

Mojave Aerospace Ventures, with SPACESHIPONE, November 2004. $10 million for the first non-government reusable manned craft to reach 62 miles twice within two weeks, carrying weight equal to three adults.
EVA and MMU
EVA = extra-vehicular activity (a space walk); the suits have their own life support. MMU = Manned Maneuvering Unit, NITROGEN-propelled, hand-controlled, allowing more mobility than tethers.
Space suits — Apollo and Shuttle
APOLLO: tailor-made suits with a SEPARATE BACKPACK life support system. SPACE SHUTTLE: lighter, more durable, easier to move in, made in standard SIZES, with life support built into the TORSO.
Compare the first Soviet and American spacewalk durations
LEONOV: about 12 MINUTES outside Voskhod II, March 1965. ED WHITE: 22 MINUTES outside Gemini IV, June 1965. The longest Apollo lunar EVA was 7 hours 37 minutes, on Apollo 17.
STS-5 — why is it significant?
Declared the FIRST OPERATIONAL Space Shuttle flight, November 1982. From orbit it deployed TWO SATELLITES.
Which Shuttle mission carried the first ESA Spacelab mission?
STS-9.
How many manned Gemini flights were there, and what did Gemini achieve?
TEN manned flights. Gemini was the FIRST TWO-MAN capsule and achieved the first AMERICAN walk in space. It also gathered information on the effects of space flight on the human body.
Compare Leonov's and the American spacewalk timing
Leonov walked in space in 1965, TWO MONTHS PRIOR to the first American walk in space.
